items.title: Home
items.text:
import useq
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()  # demo devices

sequence = useq.MDASequence(
    channels=["DAPI", "FITC"],
    time_plan={"interval": 1, "loops": 5},
)
core.mda.run(sequence, output="data.ome.zarr")

items.title: pymmcore-plus
items.text:
These docs cover pymmcore-plus and the packages built around it, which let you control a microscope from Python by talking directly to Micro-Manager's C++ core and device adapters (with no Java process involved). You can use them to script your hardware and run multi-dimensional acquisitions, or to build your own GUI (or just use one of ours).

Get started User guide

items.title: Where to start
items.text:
If you're new here, Getting Started walks you through installing things, controlling Micro-Manager's demo devices from Python, running a first acquisition, and putting together a small GUI (no microscope required). If you already know Micro-Manager, have a look at Coming from Micro-Manager, which maps what you know onto these packages.

If you'd rather not write any code, pymmcore-gui is our (work in progress) desktop application, and napari-micromanager controls a microscope from inside napari.

items.title: How the pieces fit together
items.text:
Each package builds on the ones below it. You only need to go as far up the stack as you want (pymmcore-plus on its own is enough to script a microscope).

Applications

pymmcore-gui · napari-micromanager

Desktop applications for running a microscope. Widgets

pymmcore-widgets

Qt widgets for devices, properties, configurations and acquisitions. Control & acquisition

pymmcore-plus · useq-schema

The core, extended with events and an acquisition engine, and a schema for describing experiments. Micro-Manager

pymmcore · device adapters

The C++ core and drivers for hundreds of cameras, stages, shutters, lasers, etc... Your microscope

  Micro-Manager's demo devices, or your own hardware

items.title: Getting help
items.text: If you have usage questions ("How do I...?"), please ask on the image.sc forum with the pymmcore-plus tag, or come chat with us on Zulip. Bug reports and feature requests are always welcome on GitHub (each package has its own repository; see Contributing if you're not sure which one).

items.title: API Reference
items.text:
These pages are generated from the docstrings of each package. Each object is documented once, under the shortest path you can import it from (e.g. pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus, not pymmcore_plus.core.CMMCorePlus). Other modules that re-export it just link there.

  • pymmcore-plus

    CMMCorePlus (all of the core's methods, marking what pymmcore-plus adds or changes), the acquisition engine, device objects, constants, metadata, and the mmcore command line tool.

  • useq-schema

    MDASequence, MDAEvent, and the plans for each axis (time, z, positions, grids, autofocus).

  • pymmcore-widgets

    One page for each widget, with a screenshot and an example. (The widget gallery is a quicker way to browse them.)

  • pymmcore-gui

    The application's entry points (create_mmgui) and the actions and widgets you can use to extend it.

napari-micromanager has no public Python API of its own, but you can drive it from a script (see Scripting napari-micromanager).

Release notes for each package are on GitHub: pymmcore-plus, useq-schema, pymmcore-widgets, napari-micromanager.

Linking to these docs from your own project

Each package publishes an object inventory for mkdocstrings and intersphinx, e.g. https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/objects.inv (or https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/objects.inv for everything).

items.title: Contributing
items.text: Thanks for thinking of a way to help! Remember that contributions come in all shapes and sizes beyond writing bug fixes. Improving documentation, opening issues for bugs, asking for clarification on things you find unclear, and requesting new features are all super valuable contributions.

items.title: Where things live
items.text:
Each package has its own repository, issue tracker, and contributing notes:

Package Repository Contributing notes pymmcore-plus pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus Contributing to pymmcore-plus useq-schema pymmcore-plus/useq-schema pymmcore-widgets pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-widgets Contributing to pymmcore-widgets pymmcore-gui pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-gui CONTRIBUTING.md napari-micromanager pymmcore-plus/napari-micromanager this website pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus.github.io How these docs work

Not sure where something belongs? Open it wherever seems closest (we can move issues between repositories), or ask us on the image.sc forum or Zulip.

items.title: Development setup
items.text:
We use uv in all of the repositories (but any virtual environment manager should work), and prek (or pre-commit) for linting:

git clone <your fork>
cd <repo>
uv sync
uv run prek install  # or: uv run pre-commit install
uv run pytest

Most of the tests need Micro-Manager's demo device adapters, so run uv run mmcore install once if you haven't already.

items.title: Improving the docs
items.text: Most pages have an edit button (top right) that opens the source file in the right repository. (Pages in the API reference are generated from docstrings, so edit those in the package's src/ folder.) Each package's docs live in its own docs/ folder, so a pull request that changes code can update the documentation at the same time. To preview the full site locally, see How these docs work.

items.title: How These Docs Work
items.text:
This site is put together from the docs/ folders (and docstrings) of several repositories, so that all of the packages share one navigation and search, and can link to each other. It's built with zensical by pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus.github.io (the hub).

graph LR
  subgraph members [Member repositories]
    plus[pymmcore-plus<br/>docs/ + src/]
    useq[useq-schema<br/>docs/ + src/]
    widgets[pymmcore-widgets<br/>docs/ + src/]
    more[...]
  end
  hub[hub: compose.py] --> build[build/docs + zensical.toml] --> site[pymmcore-plus.github.io]
  plus --> hub
  useq --> hub
  widgets --> hub
  more --> hub

items.title: Who owns what
items.text:
Each member repository owns:

  • docs/: its pages, written as they would be for a stand-alone site. The folder is published at /<repo-name>/, so pymmcore-plus/docs/guides/events.md becomes /pymmcore-plus/guides/events/.
  • docs/**/.nav.yml: awesome-nav files ordering the package's own section.
  • zensical.toml: what is specific to the package: mkdocstrings paths, griffe extensions, and the api-autonav settings for its API reference.
  • docs/_gen.py (optional): a script that generates content before the build, writing into git-ignored files (for example the CMMCorePlus method table or the widget screenshots).

The hub owns the theme, global settings, the landing page, Getting Started (plus a few pages that don't belong to any one package, like Using your own microscope), and the top-level navigation (docs/.nav.yml), which places member pages into the site-wide User Guide.

items.title: Previewing locally
items.text:
git clone https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus.github.io
cd pymmcore-plus.github.io
just serve          # clones members into .repos/ and serves http://localhost:8000

To edit a member's docs or code and see the result live, put a git worktree of your own clone in .repos/ instead (tools/repos.py --worktrees ~/path/to/clones, or git worktree add). Use --only pymmcore-plus,useq-schema for a faster preview of just some packages, and --no-gen to skip the generation scripts.

just check builds with --strict, which fails on any warning (broken links, unresolved cross-references, docstring problems).

items.title: The API reference
items.text:
API pages are generated from each member's api-autonav settings, with two rules on top:

  1. Each object is documented once, at its highest-level public name. pymmcore_plus.Device is documented on the pymmcore_plus page; the pymmcore_plus.core page lists it under Re-exports with a link. Cross-references to any public path ([x][pymmcore_plus.core.Device]) still resolve.
  2. Hand-written pages claim objects. If a page in docs/ renders an object with a identifier block, that page is where the object is documented, and the generated pages link to it. A hand-written page at a module's generated path (for example docs/api/pymmcore_plus/metadata/index.md) replaces the generated page.

items.title: Writing tips
items.text:
• Link to API objects with autorefs: [`CMMCorePlus`][pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus] works from any page in any repository.
  • Link to pages in other packages with relative paths (../useq-schema/schema/axes.md); they are checked when the site is built.
  • Snippets (--8<-- "examples/foo.py") are resolved relative to the member's repository root.
  • If you want a heading to be linked from other repositories, give it an explicit, namespaced id: ## Installing {#widgets-install}.

items.title: How changes get published
items.text:
• Pull requests to a member repository build the whole site with the PR's changes (failing only on warnings in that member's pages), and upload the result as an artifact you can download and browse.
  • Merges to main trigger a rebuild and deploy of the full site. The site is also rebuilt nightly.

items.title: Your First Acquisition
items.text:
A multi-dimensional acquisition (MDA) is a series of images collected across time points, stage positions, channels, z-planes, etc... In pymmcore-plus, the experiment is described with useq-schema and run by the acquisition engine.

We'll need a core with a configuration loaded:

from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()

items.title: Describing the experiment
items.text:
An MDASequence declares what to acquire. It doesn't know anything about your hardware (beyond the names of things like channel presets), and can be saved to (and loaded from) JSON or YAML.

import useq

x, y = core.getXYPosition()
z = core.getZPosition()

sequence = useq.MDASequence(
    channels=["DAPI", {"config": "FITC", "exposure": 50}],  # (1)!
    time_plan={"interval": 0.5, "loops": 3},  # (2)!
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 1},  # (3)!
    stage_positions=[(x, y, z), (x + 100, y, z)],  # (4)!
    axis_order="tpcz",  # (5)!
)

sequence.sizes       # {'t': 3, 'p': 2, 'c': 2, 'z': 5}
len(list(sequence))  # 60 events
  1. Channels are presets in the Channel configuration group (the default group), with an optional exposure in milliseconds.
  2. 3 time points, 0.5 seconds apart.
  3. A 4 µm z-stack in 1 µm steps, centered on the z of each stage position.
  4. Two (x, y, z) stage positions, in µm: the current position, and one 100 µm away in x. These are absolute stage coordinates, so on a real microscope, make sure they're somewhere safe!
  5. The nesting order, outermost first: for each time point, visit each position, and there, for each channel, take a z-stack.

Where is the z-stack?

A z-stack described with range (or above and below) is relative to the z of each stage position. If a position has no z, or the sequence has no stage positions at all, it is currently relative to z = 0, not to wherever your focus is. On a real microscope that could drive the objective a long way, which is why we pass the current z explicitly above.

Iterating over the sequence yields one MDAEvent per image, each describing what the hardware should do for that image (any field that is left unset means "leave it as it is"). See the MDASequence reference for more of what a sequence can express (grids, well plates, autofocus, per-position sub-sequences, etc...).

items.title: Running it
items.text:
@core.mda.events.frameReady.connect  # (1)!
def on_frame(image, event, metadata):
    print(event.index, image.shape)

core.mda.run(sequence, output="experiment.ome.zarr", overwrite=True)  # (2)!
  1. Connect to events to process data as it arrives. frameReady is called with the image (a numpy array), the MDAEvent and a dict of metadata.
  2. mda.run blocks until the acquisition is done. (Use core.run_mda(sequence) to run it on a background thread instead.) overwrite=True replaces experiment.ome.zarr if it already exists; without it, running the script a second time raises a FileExistsError.

... prints a line for each of the 60 images:

{'t': 0, 'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 0} (512, 512)
{'t': 0, 'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 1} (512, 512)
{'t': 0, 'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 2} (512, 512)
...
{'t': 2, 'p': 1, 'c': 1, 'z': 4} (512, 512)

items.title: Where did the data go?
items.text:
The output argument writes the images to disk as they arrive, and the extension picks the format. An .ome.zarr "file" is actually a folder. Each stage position is stored as a separate image inside it (experiment.ome.zarr/0, experiment.ome.zarr/1), as an array with dimensions (t, c, z, y, x). You can read it back with zarr (pip install zarr):

import zarr

data = zarr.open_array("experiment.ome.zarr/0/0", mode="r")
data.shape  # (3, 2, 5, 512, 512)

If you'd rather have files that you can drag into Fiji, use output="experiment.ome.tiff" (this needs the io extra: pip install "pymmcore-plus[io]"). With more than one stage position, you get one file per position, in a folder named after your output (experiment/experiment_p000.ome.tiff, experiment/experiment_p001.ome.tiff).

See Saving data for more on formats and options.

items.title: Beyond sequences
items.text:
MDASequence is just one way to make events. The engine will run any iterable of MDAEvent objects, so a plain list works too:

events = [
    useq.MDAEvent(channel="DAPI", exposure=10),
    useq.MDAEvent(channel="FITC", x_pos=x + 50, y_pos=y),
]
core.mda.run(events)

The iterable needn't even be of known length. A generator or a Queue can decide on the next event based on previous images (see Event-driven acquisition).

items.title: Next steps
items.text: The acquisition engine covers running acquisitions in more depth (pausing and cancelling, hardware triggering, etc...), and Building sequences shows more of what you can describe with an MDASequence. When you're ready for a graphical interface, have a look at your first GUI.

items.title: Your First GUI
items.text: You can either use one of the existing applications (pymmcore-gui or napari-micromanager), or build your own from pymmcore-widgets, a library of Qt widgets for controlling a CMMCorePlus.

items.title: Using an application
items.text:
pymmcore-guinapari-micromanager

Once it's installed (from GitHub, or as a bundled app for Windows and macOS), start it with the demo devices:

mmgui run --demo-config

Without --demo-config, the app starts with no devices loaded. You can load a configuration from the Devices menu, or start with mmgui -c path/to/config.cfg. See Using pymmcore-gui for more.

Once it's installed, start it with:

napari-micromanager

Then pick a configuration file at the top left of the window (or start it with napari-micromanager -c path/to/config.cfg).

items.title: Building your own
items.text:
Widgets in pymmcore-widgets use the global CMMCorePlus.instance() by default (see the tip in First steps), and they listen to the core's events, so if you change something from a script (or from another widget), they'll update to match. (A few widgets don't use a core at all. The sequence editors, like ChannelTable and MDASequenceWidget, just edit useq objects.)

You'll need pymmcore-widgets and a Qt backend, PyQt6 or PySide6 (see Installation, and PyQt6 or PySide6? if you're not sure which). The examples here import Qt from qtpy, so they run with either one.

Then combine widgets like any other Qt widgets:

from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication, QHBoxLayout, QVBoxLayout, QWidget

from pymmcore_widgets import (
    ChannelWidget,
    ExposureWidget,
    ImagePreview,
    LiveButton,
    SnapButton,
)

app = QApplication([])

core = CMMCorePlus.instance()  # (1)!
core.loadSystemConfiguration()

window = QWidget()
controls = QHBoxLayout()
controls.addWidget(ChannelWidget())
controls.addWidget(ExposureWidget())
controls.addWidget(SnapButton())
controls.addWidget(LiveButton())

layout = QVBoxLayout(window)
layout.addLayout(controls)
layout.addWidget(ImagePreview())
window.show()

app.exec()
  1. This is the core the widgets below will use, so loading the configuration here is enough for all of them. Pass mmcore=... to a widget to use a different core (the ConfigWizard calls it core=).

A slightly larger version of this example (custom_gui.py, which adds a configuration loader and a few more controls) looks like this:

items.title: Next steps
items.text: The widget gallery is the best place to find widgets for your own GUI (each one has a screenshot and a runnable example). Building a custom GUI walks through the larger example above, and Qt integration explains how to keep the GUI responsive while the hardware is busy.

items.title: First Steps
items.text:
At the heart of Micro-Manager is its core (CMMCore): a C++ library that loads your hardware configuration, talks to each device through its device adapter, and hands you images. Micro-Manager's Java application (MMStudio) is built on top of it, and pymmcore makes it available in Python.

The main object in pymmcore-plus is CMMCorePlus, an enhanced subclass of pymmcore.CMMCore. It aims to be a drop-in replacement, so if you've used pymmcore (or the mmc object in Micro-Manager's script panel), the methods you know are all still there. CMMCorePlus adds a number of things on top, and we'll look at a few of them here.

These examples use Micro-Manager's demo devices, so you don't need any hardware. You can paste them into a Python session (python, ipython or a Jupyter notebook) started in the environment where you installed pymmcore-plus, or put them in a script.

Is Micro-Manager open?

CMMCorePlus doesn't connect to a running copy of Micro-Manager; it opens the devices itself. Most hardware can only be opened by one program at a time, so close Micro-Manager (MMStudio) before you load the same configuration here. (The demo devices don't mind.) See Coming from Micro-Manager for more.

items.title: Loading a configuration
items.text:
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()  # (1)!

print(core.getLoadedDevices())
# ('DHub', 'Camera', 'Dichroic', 'Emission', 'Excitation', 'Objective', 'Z', ...)
  1. With no argument, this loads the demo configuration (MMConfig_demo.cfg). Pass the path to your own .cfg file to use your hardware (see Using your own microscope).

items.title: Snapping an image
items.text:
core.setExposure(25)  # milliseconds
image = core.snap()  # (1)!
print(image.shape, image.dtype)  # (512, 512) uint16
  1. snap is a CMMCorePlus convenience that calls snapImage() and returns getImage() as a numpy array.

image is just a numpy array, so you can look at it or save it with whatever tools you like. For example, to save it as a TIFF (that you can open in Fiji), use tifffile, which comes with the io extra (or pip install tifffile):

import tifffile

tifffile.imwrite("snap.tif", image)

(In a Jupyter notebook, matplotlib.pyplot.imshow(image) is a quick way to have a look at it.)

items.title: Reading and setting properties
items.text:
Each device has a number of properties. You can use the classic string-based API:

core.getProperty("Camera", "Binning")      # '1'
core.setProperty("Camera", "Binning", "2")
core.getImageWidth()                       # 256

...or the object-oriented Device and DeviceProperty views:

camera = core.getDeviceObject("Camera")
gain = camera.getPropertyObject("Gain")
gain.value = 1
gain.range()  # (-5.0, 8.0)

See Devices & properties for more.

items.title: Configuration groups and presets
items.text:
A configuration group (such as "Channel") holds a number of presets (such as "DAPI" or "FITC"), each of which sets several properties at once. These are the same groups and presets you'd see in Micro-Manager's main window:

core.getAvailableConfigs("Channel")   # ('Cy5', 'DAPI', 'FITC', 'Rhodamine')
core.setConfig("Channel", "FITC")
core.getCurrentConfig("Channel")      # 'FITC'

See Configuration groups for more.

items.title: Moving stages
items.text:
Positions are in microns:

core.setXYPosition(100, 200)
core.setZPosition(10)
core.waitForSystem()  # (1)!
core.getXYPosition()  # [100.005, 199.995]
  1. Stage movements may return before the hardware has finished moving. waitForSystem blocks until all devices are done.

items.title: Connecting to events
items.text:
CMMCorePlus emits events as the state of the microscope changes, and you can connect your own callbacks to them. (This is how the widgets in pymmcore-widgets stay in sync with the core.)

@core.events.propertyChanged.connect  # (1)!
def on_change(device: str, prop: str, value: str) -> None:
    print(f"{device}.{prop} changed to {value}")

core.setProperty("Camera", "Gain", "2")  # prints "Camera.Gain changed to 2"
  1. Using connect as a decorator registers the function below it as a callback. core.events.propertyChanged.connect(on_change) does the same thing.

CMMCorePlus.instance

Creating/accessing a CMMCorePlus object using CMMCorePlus.instance() is a convenient way to access the same core instance from multiple places in your code. The widgets in pymmcore-widgets also use CMMCorePlus.instance() by default, so any widgets you use will automatically connect to the same core instance without any additional configuration.

Attempts are made to make it thread-safe. But please open an issue if you find any problems.

items.title: Next steps
items.text: From here, you'll probably want to run your first acquisition. When you're ready to use a real microscope, see Using your own microscope. The User Guide covers each topic in more depth, and the CMMCorePlus reference lists all of the core's methods, marking what pymmcore-plus adds or changes.

items.title: Coming from Micro-Manager
items.text: If you've used Micro-Manager's Java application (MMStudio), much of what you know carries over. pymmcore-plus uses the same C++ core (MMCore) and the same device adapters as MMStudio, and it reads the same configuration files. What's different is everything above the core. In place of MMStudio's Java GUI and acquisition engine, you get a Python object (CMMCorePlus), an acquisition engine written in Python, and (if you want a GUI) widgets and applications written in Python.

items.title: One program at a time
items.text:
pymmcore-plus doesn't connect to a running copy of Micro-Manager; it replaces it. Each program loads its own copy of the core, and the core opens your devices itself (serial ports, camera drivers, etc...). Most devices can only be opened by one program at a time, so if MMStudio has your configuration loaded, loading it again from Python will usually fail (and if it doesn't, the two programs will be fighting over the same hardware). So please close MMStudio before you load your configuration in Python, and vice versa. (The demo devices don't mind, so it's fine to have both open while you're trying things out.)

If you want to keep using MMStudio and control it from Python at the same time, that's what Pycro-Manager is for (see below).

items.title: Where things went
items.text:
In MMStudio Here Hardware Configuration Wizard and .cfg files The same files: core.loadSystemConfiguration("MyScope.cfg"). See Using your own microscope. Device Property Browser core.getProperty() and core.setProperty(), or the PropertyBrowser widget Groups and presets (main window) core.setConfig("Channel", "FITC"), or GroupPresetTableWidget Snap and Live core.snap() and core.startContinuousSequenceAcquisition(), or SnapButton and LiveButton Multi-D Acquisition window Describe the experiment with a useq.MDASequence and run it with core.mda.run() (see Your first acquisition), or use the MDAWidget Stage Position List stage_positions in an MDASequence Saving acquisitions core.mda.run(sequence, output="data.ome.zarr") (or .ome.tiff). See Saving data. Pixel Size Calibration The same pixel size presets in your .cfg file (core.getPixelSizeUm()), or the PixelConfigurationWidget Script panel (Beanshell) Python (see below) Device adapters (the mmgr_dal_* files) The very same files. mmcore install downloads them for you.

If you'd rather have all of this in one window, pymmcore-gui is our (work in progress) pure-Python replacement for MMStudio.

items.title: Scripts
items.text:
CMMCorePlus has the same methods as the core object (mmc) in MMStudio's script panel, so Beanshell scripts translate to Python almost line by line:

Beanshell (MMStudio)Python 
mmc.setConfig("Channel", "FITC");
mmc.setExposure(50);
mmc.snapImage();
img = mmc.getImage();

from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance()
mmc.loadSystemConfiguration()  # (1)!
mmc.setConfig("Channel", "FITC")
mmc.setExposure(50)
mmc.snapImage()
img = mmc.getImage()  # a numpy array
  1. MMStudio had already done this for you. Pass the path to your own .cfg file (with no argument, this loads the demo devices).

A few things are different: images come back as numpy arrays (rather than Java arrays), lists of strings come back as Python tuples (rather than StrVectors), and CMMCorePlus adds a number of conveniences on top (like snap(), which does the last two lines in one go). The mm object (MMStudio's own API for displays, data stores, the acquisition manager, etc...) is part of the Java GUI, so it has no equivalent here.

If you're working inside one of our applications, the core is already there for you. In pymmcore-gui's console it's called mmc (just like in MMStudio), and in napari-micromanager's console it's mmcore.

items.title: How is this different from Pycro-Manager?
items.text:
A common question about pymmcore-plus and related libraries is how they differ from Pycro-Manager, another Python library written by Henry Pinkard for working with Micro-Manager.

The two projects are not mutually exclusive! They aim to support different use cases.

The primary difference is that Pycro-Manager (with its default Java backend) controls Micro-Manager via a ZMQ-based connection to a remote Java process in which the Micro-Manager GUI is running (or a headless Java process if the GUI is not running). The Java process in turn communicates with the C++ core driving the hardware.

pymmcore-plus aims to remove the need for a Java process by communicating directly with the C++ core (via the pymmcore library), and re-implementing any necessary event-based or GUI-based functionality in pure Python or C.

A major advantage of Pycro-Manager is that you get the entire Java-based Micro-Manager ecosystem, including the GUI and plugins. A potential disadvantage (depending on your needs) is that it requires a Java runtime environment and cross-process communication.

(Pycro-Manager has since added a Python backend for its headless mode, which also runs the core inside the Python process via pymmcore, along with a Python version of its acquisition engine. It's a separate project from pymmcore-plus, with its own API.)

If you are looking to control a microscope via Python without any need for Java or interprocess communication, pymmcore-plus may help. Note, however, that you will be sacrificing the MMStudio GUI! See pymmcore-gui, napari-micromanager and pymmcore-widgets for our ongoing efforts to implement a complete Python-based GUI for Micro-Manager.

If you've been using Pycro-Manager and like its API, see A Pycro-Manager-style API for an example of what that could look like on top of pymmcore-plus.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
There are two things to install: the Python package(s) you want, and Micro-Manager's device adapters (the C++ drivers for your hardware). The device adapters include a set of demo devices, so you can try out the examples in these docs without a microscope.

You'll need Python 3.11 or newer.

Where do I type these commands?

In a terminal (on Windows, PowerShell or the Anaconda Prompt). We recommend installing into a fresh environment rather than into your system Python. For example, with conda:

conda create -n pymm python=3.12
conda activate pymm

... or with uv, in the folder you'll be working in:

uv venv  # creates a .venv folder here

The uv add command in the uv tab below adds a dependency to a uv project (a folder with a pyproject.toml, which uv init creates). If you just made an environment with uv venv, use uv pip install in place of uv add. Either way, uv run <command> runs a command in that environment (e.g. uv run python my_script.py).

items.title: Installing the packages
items.text:
Pick what you need, and copy the commands:

pipuv 
pip install "pymmcore-plus[cli]"

uv add "pymmcore-plus[cli]"

The parts in square brackets are optional extras. cli makes sure you get the mmcore command line tool (it's currently included anyway), and io adds support for saving OME-TIFF files. (Saving to OME-Zarr works without it.)

All install options You want Command The core library and the mmcore CLI pip install "pymmcore-plus[cli]" … plus OME-TIFF writing (and tifffile) pip install "pymmcore-plus[cli,io]" Qt widgets (choose a Qt backend) pip install "pymmcore-widgets[PyQt6]" or "pymmcore-widgets[PySide6]" The pymmcore-gui application (needs git) pip install git+https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-gui The napari plugin pip install "napari-micromanager[PyQt6]"

Each package brings in everything it builds on, so you only need the top-most one: pymmcore-gui already includes pymmcore-widgets, pymmcore-plus[cli,io] and PyQt6; napari-micromanager and pymmcore-widgets include pymmcore-plus[cli].

All of these are on PyPI. (Some are on conda-forge too, but those packages are currently out of date, so please use pip inside your conda environment.)

items.title: Installing the device adapters
items.text:
The mmcore command downloads the latest compatible Micro-Manager device adapters for your platform:

mmcore install

(If you used uv venv, that's uv run mmcore install.)

They go into a folder in your user data directory, where pymmcore-plus will find them automatically. For more details (choosing a version, using an existing Micro-Manager installation, and what the "device interface version" is), see Micro-Manager device adapters.

Apple Silicon and Linux

On Apple Silicon Macs and on Linux, mmcore install currently downloads only Micro-Manager's test adapters (the demo camera and a few others). That's all you need for the examples in these docs. For real hardware on those platforms, see Using your own microscope.

items.title: Checking your setup
items.text:
mmcore info prints the versions of the relevant packages, and the folder that the device adapters will be loaded from:

$ mmcore info
python            : 3.14.2 (main, Dec  9 2025, 19:29:30) [Clang 21.1.4 ]
platform          : macOS-27.0.1-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O
pymmcore-plus     : 0.18.1
pymmcore          : 12.5.1.75.0
pymmcore-nano     :
core-version-info : MMCore version 12.5.1
api-version-info  : Device API version 75, Module API version 10
adapter-path      : ~/Library/Application Support/pymmcore-plus/mm/Micro-Manager-75.20260226
useq-schema       : 0.9.2

If adapter-path says not found, pymmcore-plus can't find any device adapters (did mmcore install work?). If something else went wrong, have a look at Troubleshooting, and please let us know on image.sc if that doesn't help.

items.title: Next steps
items.text: Once that's done, head to First steps to start controlling the demo devices from Python, or jump straight to your first acquisition or your first GUI.

items.title: Which Package Do I Need?
items.text:
There are five packages here, each building on the ones below it (see the stack on the home page). Most people only need one of them:

If you want to… Use Start here Control a microscope with a point-and-click app pymmcore-gui pymmcore-gui Control a microscope from inside napari napari-micromanager napari-micromanager Script your microscope from Python or Jupyter pymmcore-plus First steps Run multi-dimensional acquisitions from code pymmcore-plus (includes useq-schema) Your first acquisition Describe experiments independently of any hardware useq-schema Describing experiments Build your own Qt GUI for a microscope pymmcore-widgets Your first GUI

(A multi-dimensional acquisition, or MDA, is a series of images across time points, stage positions, channels, z-planes, etc... It's what Micro-Manager's Multi-D Acquisition window does.)

Installing a package also installs the ones it builds on (pip install pymmcore-widgets gets you pymmcore-plus, useq-schema and pymmcore too). The Micro-Manager device adapters (the drivers for your hardware) are not Python packages, though, and always need to be installed separately. Installation covers both, so whichever package you pick, start there.

If you've used Micro-Manager before, you may also want to read Coming from Micro-Manager.

items.title: What each package does
items.text: pymmcore-plus Extends pymmcore, the Python bindings for Micro-Manager's C++ core. CMMCorePlus aims to be a drop-in replacement for CMMCore, adding an event system, an acquisition engine written in Python, and a number of convenience methods. It also provides the mmcore command line tool. useq-schema A schema for describing multi-dimensional acquisitions (MDASequence, MDAEvent). It tries to stay agnostic to the acquisition engine (though it was designed around what Micro-Manager can do). pymmcore-widgets Qt widgets for a CMMCorePlus: property browsers, device controls, configuration editors, MDA editors, image previews, etc... pymmcore-gui A desktop application built from all of the above (plus the ndv viewer). The goal is a pure-Python replacement for Micro-Manager's Java GUI. It's still early days, so expect some rough edges. napari-micromanager A napari plugin for controlling a microscope from the napari viewer. It's still maintained, but current development is focused on pymmcore-gui.

items.title: User Guide
items.text:
The User Guide is organized by topic, roughly following the stack from the hardware up. Each page belongs to one package's docs (the badge at the top says which), and names of classes and functions link to the API reference. If you're new here, Getting Started is probably a better place to begin.

  • Controlling hardware

    Installing device adapters, using your own microscope, devices and properties, configuration groups, and events and callbacks (which are how GUIs, and your own code, stay in sync with the core).

  • Describing experiments

    How useq-schema describes an acquisition as a sequence of events, and building sequences with time points, z-stacks, channels, positions, grids, etc...

  • Running acquisitions

    The acquisition engine, saving data, event-driven acquisition, and writing your own engine.

  • Building GUIs

    The widget gallery, building a custom GUI from those widgets, and keeping it responsive.

  • Applications

    pymmcore-gui, our desktop application, and napari-micromanager, which controls a microscope from inside napari.

  • Advanced topics

    Device adapters written in Python (UniMMCore), a preview of useq-schema v2, and a Pycro-Manager-style API.

Something not working?

The troubleshooting pages cover the core and device adapters and Qt and widgets. Turning up the logging (or profiling, if things are slow) can also help you work out what's going on. If you're still stuck, please ask on the image.sc forum.

items.title: Using Your Own Microscope
items.text:
Getting Started uses Micro-Manager's demo devices throughout. To control real hardware, you need two more things: the device adapters for your hardware, and a configuration file that says which devices you have and how they're set up.

(If Micro-Manager is running and connected to the same hardware, close it first. See One program at a time.)

items.title: What's a configuration file?
items.text:
A Micro-Manager configuration file (.cfg) is a plain text file listing the devices to load (and which device adapter each one comes from), their initial property values, which device plays which role (camera, shutter, focus stage), and the configuration groups, presets and pixel sizes you've defined. Here are a few lines from the demo configuration, MMConfig_demo.cfg:

# Devices
Device,Camera,DemoCamera,DCam
Device,Z,DemoCamera,DStage
Device,XY,DemoCamera,DXYStage
...
# Roles
Property,Core,Camera,Camera
Property,Core,Focus,Z
...
# Group: Channel
# Preset: FITC
ConfigGroup,Channel,FITC,Dichroic,Label,Q505LP
ConfigGroup,Channel,FITC,Emission,Label,Chroma-HQ535
...
PixelSize_um,Res10x,1.0

You rarely need to edit one by hand. If you already have a configuration file from Micro-Manager, you can use it as it is (both use the same core, so they read the same files). Micro-Manager's configuration guide describes the format in detail.

items.title: Making a configuration file
items.text:
The Hardware Configuration Wizard walks you through adding your devices, setting their properties, assigning roles and saving the file. There are three versions of it, and you can use whichever is handiest:

  • In pymmcore-gui: Devices > Hardware Config Wizard...

  • As a widget in your own Python code, ConfigWizard:

    from pymmcore_widgets import ConfigWizard
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

app = QApplication([])
wizard = ConfigWizard()  # (1)!
wizard.show()
app.exec()
    1. Pass config_file="MyScope.cfg" to start from an existing file. Like most widgets, it uses CMMCorePlus.instance() unless you pass a core (here, the argument is called core=).

  • In Micro-Manager itself: Devices > Hardware Configuration Wizard.... If mmcore install downloaded a full Micro-Manager for you (on Windows and Intel Macs), mmcore mmstudio will start it.

items.title: Getting the device adapters
items.text:
On Windows and Intel Macs, mmcore install downloads a complete Micro-Manager nightly build, which includes the device adapters for most supported hardware. On Apple Silicon Macs and on Linux, it currently downloads only the test adapters (DemoCamera, Utilities and a few others), so for real hardware on those platforms you'll need to build the adapters you need from source.

If you already have Micro-Manager installed (with the adapters you need), pymmcore-plus can use it, as long as its device interface version matches the one your pymmcore expects. mmcore list shows the installations it found (and which of them are compatible), and mmcore use <path> picks one. See Micro-Manager device adapters for more on all of this.

Some devices also need the manufacturer's own drivers or SDK installed (many cameras do, for example). Micro-Manager's device support pages say what each adapter needs.

items.title: Loading it
items.text:
In Python, pass the path to loadSystemConfiguration:

from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration("path/to/MyScope.cfg")  # (1)!
  1. Relative paths are looked for in the current directory first, then in the device adapter folder.

Both applications can load a configuration at startup:

mmgui -c path/to/MyScope.cfg                # pymmcore-gui
napari-micromanager -c path/to/MyScope.cfg  # napari-micromanager

... and mmcore bench -c path/to/MyScope.cfg times a few basic operations on each of your devices, which is a quick way to check that they load.

If loading fails, the error message usually names the device that couldn't be initialized. mmcore logs shows the end of the log file (which has more detail), and Troubleshooting covers the most common problems.

If you change the configuration from Python (for example, by defining new presets), core.saveSystemConfiguration("MyScope.cfg") writes it back out.

items.title: Groups, channels and pixel sizes
items.text:
Once the devices are loaded, most day-to-day settings live in configuration groups and their presets (see Configuration groups). When you list channels in an MDASequence, they're looked up in a group named Channel by default. If your channel group has a different name, say so:

import useq

useq.MDASequence(channels=[{"config": "DAPI", "group": "Filters"}])

Pixel sizes are stored in the configuration file too, as presets tied to your objectives, and the core picks the right one as the objective changes. With the demo configuration:

core.getAvailablePixelSizeConfigs()  # ('Res10x', 'Res20x', 'Res40x')
core.setConfig("Objective", "20X")
core.getPixelSizeUm()                # 0.5

You can set these up with the PixelConfigurationWidget (in pymmcore-gui, Window > Pixel Size Configuration), and then save the configuration.

items.title: napari-micromanager
items.text:
napari-micromanager is a napari plugin that turns napari into a microscope control application, powered by pymmcore-plus and pymmcore-widgets. Images you snap or acquire show up as napari layers, right next to whatever analysis you do in napari.

Development has moved to pymmcore-gui

napari-micromanager continues to be maintained, but current development is focused on pymmcore-gui, a napari-independent application (using ndv for viewing), for reasons of performance and fewer dependencies. If you don't need napari, start with pymmcore-gui.

  • Installing and launching the plugin.
  • Scripting: drive napari-micromanager from Python.

items.title: Installing napari-micromanager
items.text:
pip install "napari-micromanager[PyQt6]"
# or, for the PySide6 Qt backend: pip install "napari-micromanager[PySide6]"

(The quotes keep zsh, the default shell on macOS, from complaining about the square brackets.) If you've already installed napari with a Qt backend in this environment (e.g. pip install "napari[all]"), plain pip install napari-micromanager is enough.

You will then also need to grab the Micro-Manager device adapters:

mmcore install

See Installing Micro-Manager device adapters for details on the mmcore helper command.

items.title: Usage
items.text:
napari-micromanager

This will open a new napari window with the micromanager plugin enabled. To load a configuration file right away, pass it with -c:

napari-micromanager -c path/to/config.cfg
napari-micromanager -c MMConfig_demo.cfg  # Micro-Manager's demo devices

Otherwise, select a MM Config file at the top left of the window, then click load. (You can also add the plugin to a napari window that's already open, from the Plugins menu, or start napari with it: napari -w napari-micromanager.)

The plugin adds a row of toolbars along the top of the napari window: the configuration file, the channel group and channel, the objective, the shutters, Snap and Live, and the exposure time. The buttons at the end of the row open more panels, docked in the napari window: the device property browser, configuration groups and presets, illumination, stage control, camera ROI, pixel size, and MDA for multi-dimensional acquisitions. Snapped and live images go to a napari layer called "preview", and each acquisition gets layers of its own, so you can use any napari tool or plugin on them. A MinMax panel shows the minimum and maximum pixel values of the layers. Then ... much of the rest is hopefully self explanatory .

Underlying napari-micromanager is the pymmcore-plus package, which is a python wrapper around pymmcore and the C++ CMMCore library (not pycro-manager and not the Java-based MMStudio). See the User Guide for more on pymmcore-plus; the widgets in the GUI are all powered by pymmcore-widgets.

items.title: Scripting napari-micromanager
items.text:
napari-micromanager creates and owns its own CMMCorePlus. (It deliberately does not use the global CMMCorePlus.instance(), so a core you configured with CMMCorePlus.instance() is not the one the plugin drives.) Once you have a reference to the plugin's core, anything you can do with pymmcore-plus can be combined with the GUI. There are a few ways to get it:

  • main_window.core, where main_window is the plugin's MainWindow (see the script below);
  • napari_micromanager.get_core(), which finds the plugin in the current napari viewer;
  • in napari's console, the variable mmcore (see below).

items.title: Launching napari from a script
items.text:
For complex scripting you will likely want to launch napari from a script or a Jupyter notebook:

examples/launch_from_script.py
import napari

v = napari.Viewer()
dw, main_window = v.window.add_plugin_dock_widget("napari-micromanager")

# the CMMCorePlus instance that napari-micromanager is driving
mmc = main_window.core

# do any complicated scripting you want here
...

# start napari
napari.run()

items.title: Using a core you created
items.text:
To have the plugin drive a core that you created and configured yourself, pass it as mmcore when you create the MainWindow, and add that to the viewer:

import napari
from napari_micromanager import MainWindow
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()  # or your own configuration file

viewer = napari.Viewer()
main_window = MainWindow(viewer, mmcore=core)
viewer.window.add_dock_widget(main_window, name="MicroManager", area="top")

napari.run()

The plugin then leaves the core's lifecycle to you. When the window closes, it doesn't cancel a running acquisition or unload the devices, as it does for a core it created itself.

items.title: Using the integrated napari console
items.text:
After launching napari and starting the napari-micromanager plugin, open the napari console (the >_ button at the bottom left of the window). It already defines mmcore, the core the plugin is driving, along with MDASequence and MDAEvent from useq, so you can run an acquisition from there:

mmcore.run_mda(MDASequence(time_plan={"interval": 1, "loops": 5}))

items.title: pymmcore-gui
items.text:
pymmcore-gui is a desktop application for controlling microscopes with the Micro-Manager core, written in Python. It's built from the other packages on this site (plus ndv for viewing images), and the goal is to provide a pure-Python replacement for Micro-Manager's Java GUI (MMStudio).

Name pending

pymmcore-gui is a working title. The application is usable today, but expect rough edges and frequent changes.

items.title: Who it's for
items.text:
pymmcore-gui is for people who want to use a microscope from a Python application the way they'd use MMStudio: load a configuration, look at the live image, set up a multi-dimensional acquisition and run it, without writing code. It's also a place to start if you're a developer who'd rather add a few panels to an existing application than build a GUI from scratch with pymmcore-widgets. You can add your own widgets, and script the running GUI from its built-in console.

pymmcore-gui or napari-micromanager?

napari-micromanager came first. It's a napari plugin built from the same widgets, in which images become napari layers. It's still maintained, but new development is going into pymmcore-gui, which uses ndv instead of napari (for performance, and to keep the dependencies down). If your analysis already lives in napari, napari-micromanager may suit you better; otherwise, start with pymmcore-gui.

items.title: What's inside
items.text: Component Role in the GUI pymmcore-plus Device control and the acquisition engine (CMMCorePlus, MDAEngine). useq-schema Describes the experiments you run: time-lapses, z-stacks, channels, well plates, grids, ... pymmcore-widgets The panels: camera and stage control, property browser, acquisition setup, ... ndv Fast, lightweight n-dimensional viewer for live and acquired images.

items.title: Features
items.text:
• Device control and configuration (including the Hardware Configuration Wizard)
  • Multi-dimensional acquisitions: time, z, channels, positions, grids, well plates
  • Real-time image preview and acquisition visualization (2D and 3D)
  • Customizable, dockable layouts
  • An integrated IPython console with access to the running core
  • Double-clickable application bundles for Windows and macOS

items.title: Next steps
items.text: To try it out, install pymmcore-gui (as a Python package or a bundled app), then see Using pymmcore-gui for launching it, its command-line options, and scripting it from Python. The API reference documents the parts you can build on.

items.title: Installing pymmcore-gui
items.text:
There are two ways to get pymmcore-gui: as a Python package, or as a bundled, double-clickable application.

Python packageBundled application

You'll need Python 3.11 or newer, and git (pip uses it to fetch the code).

# install the latest version from GitHub
pip install git+https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-gui

# install Micro-Manager device adapters
mmcore install

# run the app (with the demo devices)
mmgui run --demo-config

Or run it without installing anything permanently, using uv:

uvx --from git+https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-gui mmgui

pymmcore-gui isn't released on PyPI yet. (There is a pymmcore-gui package there, but it's an outdated pre-release, so please install from GitHub.)

pymmcore-gui requires a specific version of PyQt6, so install it in its own environment rather than next to another Qt application (or a PySide6 project).

Tip

The GitHub version may change at any time, so pin a specific commit if you add it to your own dependencies: pymmcore-gui @ git+https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-gui@<commit>

Pre-built bundles include the Python runtime and all dependencies. Download and extract the archive, then run the application.

Platform Latest nightly build Windows pymmgui-Windows.zip macOS pymmgui-macOS.zip

Unsigned app

Until the bundles are signed, your OS will warn you about running an app from an unidentified developer; you will need to accept that warning.

items.title: Micro-Manager device adapters
items.text:
Neither option includes the Micro-Manager device adapters (the drivers for your hardware). Install them in one of these ways:

  • Use the Devices > Install Devices... menu in the GUI.
  • Run mmcore install (or uvx --from "pymmcore-plus[cli]" mmcore install).
  • Install a Micro-Manager nightly build.

See Installing Micro-Manager device adapters for details.

License

The bundled application includes PyQt6 (GPL-3.0), so the bundle is distributed as a combined work under the GPL-3.0. pymmcore-gui itself is BSD-3-Clause.

items.title: Launching the app
items.text:
Double-click the bundled application, or run mmgui from a terminal in the environment where you installed pymmcore-gui.

On first launch, no configuration is loaded, so there isn't much to control yet. To try the GUI without hardware, load Micro-Manager's demo devices with Devices > Load Demo Configuration, or start the app with them:

mmgui run --demo-config

Load your own configuration from Devices > Load System Configuration..., or create one with the Hardware Configuration Wizard (Devices > Hardware Config Wizard...). On later launches, the GUI offers to reload the last configuration you used.

Error reports

The first time you launch it, the app asks whether you'd like to send error reports to the developers (through Sentry). This is opt-in: nothing is sent unless you agree, and the privacy policy lists what's included. Your answer is saved in the app's settings (mmgui settings --reset clears it). Starting the app with mmgui run --no-telemetry skips the question and doesn't send anything.

items.title: Command-line options
items.text:
mmgui is short for mmgui run, which starts the app. It takes these options:

Option What it does -c FILE, --config FILE Load this Micro-Manager configuration file. --demo-config Load Micro-Manager's demo configuration. --no-telemetry Don't ask about (or send) error reports.

For example, mmgui run -c path/to/my_scope.cfg. (Spell out run when you pass options. Plain mmgui -c FILE works, but mmgui --demo-config does not.)

The app keeps its settings (window layout, last configuration, your answer about error reports) in a settings file. mmgui settings --edit opens that file, mmgui settings --reveal shows it in your file browser, and mmgui settings --reset restores the defaults. mmgui --version prints the versions of pymmcore-gui, pymmcore-plus and pymmcore.

items.title: The console
items.text:
The Console (in the Window menu, and the >_ button in the toolbar) is an IPython console running in the app itself. It predefines a few names, so you can script the running GUI:

  • mmc (also core and mmcore): the CMMCorePlus the GUI is using;
  • mda: its acquisition runner (mmc.mda);
  • window: the main window;
  • np, useq, and the top-level names from pymmcore_plus and useq (MDASequence, ...).

For example, mmc.setExposure(50) updates the exposure everywhere in the GUI.

items.title: Launching from Python
items.text:
Start the GUI from a script or an interactive session with create_mmgui:

from pymmcore_gui import create_mmgui

create_mmgui()

This call blocks until the window is closed (it runs the Qt event loop).

items.title: Customizing before launch
items.text:
Pass exec_app=False to get the main window back before the Qt event loop starts, customize it, then start the event loop yourself. (You don't need to create a QApplication, because create_mmgui makes one for you.)

from pymmcore_gui import create_mmgui
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

window = create_mmgui(exec_app=False)

# customize the window, or script the core it uses:
mmcore = window.mmcore

QApplication.instance().exec()

items.title: Using your own core
items.text:
By default, the GUI uses the global CMMCorePlus.instance(), creating it if needed, so any script can reach the same core the GUI is driving. If you already have a CMMCorePlus instance with a configuration loaded, pass it in, along with mm_config=False:

from pymmcore_gui import create_mmgui
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

my_core = CMMCorePlus()
my_core.loadSystemConfiguration()  # or your own configuration file

create_mmgui(mmcore=my_core, mm_config=False)

Without mm_config=False, the GUI goes through its usual startup logic, and may load (or offer to load) the last configuration you used on top of the one you set up.

items.title: Adding your own widget
items.text:
Experimental

Clearer paths for customizing the interface are on the to-do list, so this may change.

The panels in the Window menu are registered as WidgetActionInfo objects, and you can register your own. Give it a unique key, the text to show in the menu, and a function that takes the main window (the parent) and returns your widget. Register it before calling create_mmgui, and it shows up in the Window menu, and opens as a dockable panel:

from pymmcore_gui import create_mmgui
from pymmcore_gui.actions import WidgetActionInfo
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication, QLabel


def make_notes(parent):
    return QLabel("Remember to turn off the laser!", parent)


WidgetActionInfo(key="mylab.notes", text="Lab Notes", create_widget=make_notes)

window = create_mmgui(exec_app=False)
window.get_widget("mylab.notes")  # (optional) open it right away
QApplication.instance().exec()

Widgets from pymmcore-widgets work too. The parent passed to your function is the main window, so you can hand them the GUI's core: ExposureWidget(parent=parent, mmcore=parent.mmcore).

items.text:
create_mmgui(
    *,
    mm_config: Path | str | None | Literal[False] = None,
    mmcore: CMMCorePlus | None = None,
    install_sys_excepthook: bool = True,
    install_sentry: bool = True,
    exec_app: bool = True,
) -> MicroManagerGUI

Initialize the pymmcore-gui application and Main Window.

This is the primary way to start pymmcore-gui. (It is also called by __main__.main() when running from the command line.)

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mm_config str | None | False

The path to the Micro-Manager configuration file to load. - If False, no configuration will be loaded. - If a non-empty string, that configuration will be loaded. - If None (or the empty string), auto-deciding logic will be used based on the stored user settings (based on the settings values for Settings.last_config and Settings.auto_load_last_config).

None mmcore CMMCorePlus | None

The CMMCorePlus instance to use. If None (default), the global CMMCorePlus.instance() will be used if it exists, or a new (global) instance will be created (which you may access later with CMMCorePlus.instance()). Note: you may wish to also pass mm_config = False to prevent loading a system configuration, if you have already loaded one in your instance.

None install_sys_excepthook bool

If True (the default), installs a custom excepthook that does not raise sys.exit(). This is necessary to prevent the application from closing when an unhandled exception is raised in the main thread.

True install_sentry bool

If True (the default), the user will be given an option to send error reports to the developers, unless they have previously opted in/out. If False, no prompt will be shown, and no error reports will be sent.

True exec_app bool

If True (the default), the QApplication event loop will be started. If False, the event loop will not be started, and the caller is responsible for starting it with QApplication.instance().exec().

True

items.title: pymmcore-plus
items.text:
pymmcore-plus aims to extend pymmcore (Python bindings for the C++ Micro-Manager core) with a number of features designed to facilitate working with Micro-Manager in pure Python/C environments. The main object in this library, CMMCorePlus, aims to be a drop-in replacement for pymmcore.CMMCore, while adding a number of additional features including:

  • A multi-dimensional acquisition engine implemented in pure Python. (The existing acquisition engines in Micro-Manager are written in Java and Clojure.)
  • More flexible event connections and callback handling.
  • Extended convenience APIs for working with the core (which would be hard or impossible to implement in the pymmcore SWIG wrapper).
  • More pythonic APIs for various pymmcore objects (e.g. Device, Configuration) and constants.

items.title: Where to start
items.text: If you're new here, start with Installation (which includes getting the Micro-Manager device adapters), then First steps and Your first acquisition. The User Guide goes into more depth on devices and properties, configuration groups, events, running acquisitions and saving data.

items.title: Reference
items.text:
• CMMCorePlus: every method of the core, with what pymmcore-plus adds or overrides marked.
  • pymmcore_plus.mda: the acquisition runner (MDARunner) and engine (MDAEngine).
  • Events: the signals emitted by core.events and core.mda.events.
  • Metadata schema: the metadata dicts that come with each acquired frame.
  • Constants: the enums that replace pymmcore's integer constants.
  • Command line (mmcore) and environment variables.

items.title: CLI Reference
items.text:
This page provides documentation for the mmcore command line tool, which is installed along with pymmcore-plus.

The CLI can be used to interact with the pymmcore_plus package from the command line, including the installation, removal, and selection of Micro-Manager device adapters, showing log files, and running a test acquisition (mmcore run, which doesn't save anything). (The default --dest folder for install and build-dev depends on your platform; see Micro-Manager device adapters.)

items.title: mmcore
items.text:
mmcore: pymmcore-plus command line.

For additional help on a specific command: type mmcore COMMAND --help

Usage:

$ mmcore [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

Options:

  • --version: Show version and exit.
  • --install-completion: Install completion for the current shell.
  • --show-completion: Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

items.title: mmcore clean
items.text:
Remove all Micro-Manager installs downloaded by pymmcore-plus.

Usage:

$ mmcore clean [OPTIONS] [glob]

Arguments:

  • glob: glob pattern to clean [default: *]

Options:

  • --help: Show this message and exit.

items.title: mmcore list
items.text:
Show all discovered Micro-Manager installations.

Usage:

$ mmcore list [OPTIONS]

Options:

  • --help: Show this message and exit.

items.title: mmcore mmstudio
items.text:
Run the Java Micro-Manager GUI.

This command will attempt to locate and execute an ImageJ application found in the active Micro-Manager directory.

Usage:

$ mmcore mmstudio [OPTIONS]

Options:

  • --help: Show this message and exit.

items.title: mmcore install
items.text:
Install Micro-Manager device adapters from https://download.micro-manager.org.

On Windows and Intel macOS, this downloads a nightly build of Micro-Manager. Micro-Manager doesn't publish nightly builds for Linux or Apple Silicon, so on those platforms only the test adapters (DemoCamera, Utilities, etc...) are installed, from https://github.com/micro-manager/mm-test-adapters.

Usage:

$ mmcore install [OPTIONS]

Options:

  • -d, --dest <directory>: Installation directory. [default: <user data dir>/pymmcore-plus/mm]
  • -r, --release <str>: Release date. e.g. 20210201 [default: latest-compatible]
  • --plain-output: Do not use rich output. Useful for scripting.
  • --test-adapters: Install only test adapters (e.g. DemoCamera and others for testing).
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

items.title: mmcore run
items.text:
Run a Micro-Manager acquisition from a useq-schema MDASequence file.

Nothing is saved to disk (this is mostly useful for testing and profiling).

Usage:

$ mmcore run [OPTIONS] [useq]

Arguments:

  • useq: Path to useq-schema file.

Options:

  • -c, --config <file>: Path to Micro-Manager system configuration file.
  • --z-go-up / --no-z-go-up: Acquire from bottom to top.
  • --z-top <float>: Top of z-stack.
  • --z-bottom <float>: Bottom of z-stack.
  • --z-range <float>: Symmetric range of z-stack around position.
  • --z-above <float>: Asymmetric range of z-stack above position.
  • --z-below <float>: Asymmetric range of z-stack below position.
  • --z-step <float>: Step size of z-stack.
  • -zr <float>: Relative z-positions to acquire (may use multiple times).
  • -za <float>: Absolute z-positions to acquire (may use multiple times).
  • --t-interval <float>: Interval between timepoints.
  • --t-duration <float>: Duration of time lapse.
  • --t-loops <float>: Number of time points to acquire.
  • --dry-run / --no-dry-run: Do not run the acquisition. [default: no-dry-run]
  • --axis-order <str>: Order of axes to acquire (e.g. 'TPCZ').
  • --channel <str>: Channel to acquire. Argument is a string of the following form:
    • name: "DAPI"
    • name;exposure: "DAPI;0.5"
    • useq-schema JSON: '{"config": "DAPI", "exposure": 0.5, "z_offset": 0.5}'
  • --channel-group <str>: Name of Micro-Manager configuration group for channels. [default: Channel]
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

items.title: mmcore build-dev
items.text:
Build Micro-Manager device adapters from the git repo.

Currently only supports macos and linux.

Usage:

$ mmcore build-dev [OPTIONS] [devices]...

Arguments:

items.title: Contributing to pymmcore-plus
items.text: All development for this library happens in the pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus repo on GitHub. The general setup (cloning, uv sync, prek, running the tests) is the same as for the other packages, and is described on the main Contributing page. This page has a few notes that are specific to pymmcore-plus.

items.title: Without uv
items.text:
If you're using a different virtual environment manager (like conda) instead of uv, you can install the package and its development dependencies with:

pip install -e . --group dev

This requires a newer version of pip (>= 25.1) to work.

items.title: Device adapters for the tests
items.text:
Most of the tests use Micro-Manager's demo devices, so you'll need a compatible set of device adapters:

uv run mmcore install

On Linux and Apple Silicon this installs just the test adapters (which is all the tests need). Alternatively, pip install mm-test-adapters puts them in your environment, where pymmcore-plus will find them (this can be handy on CI). You can confirm that everything works by running:

from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()
core.snap()

If you want to test against device adapters built from the current mmCoreAndDevices source (on macOS or Linux), run uv run mmcore build-dev. This will download the micro-manager repo, build it, and drop the DemoCamera, Utilities and SequenceTester devices into the pymmcore-plus user data folder (by default ~/Library/Application Support/pymmcore-plus/mm on macOS), which is on the default search path. (On macOS you must have homebrew installed.)

items.title: Contributing documentation
items.text: These docs live in the docs/ folder of this repository (and in docstrings), but the site itself is built by pymmcore-plus.github.io, which combines the docs of all the pymmcore-plus packages. See How these docs work to preview your changes locally. The CMMCorePlus method table and the CLI reference are generated by docs/_gen.py.

items.title: Environment Variables
items.text:
The following environment variables may be used to configure pymmcore-plus globally.

Unless noted otherwise, boolean variables can be set to 1, 0, True, or False (case insensitive).

Variable Description Default PYMM_DEBUG_LOG Call enableDebugLog(True) when creating a CMMCorePlus. PYMM_STDERR_LOG Call enableStderrLog(True) when creating a CMMCorePlus. PYMM_BUFFER_SIZE_MB Circular buffer memory footprint in MB. MMCore's default (250 MB) PYMM_STRICT_INIT_CHECKS Enable/disable strict initialization checks Enabled PYMM_PARALLEL_INIT Enable/disable parallel device initialization Enabled PYMM_LOG_LEVEL pymmcore-plus logging level for the console. 'WARNING' PYMM_LOG_FILE Logfile location. Set to 0, false, no or none to disable logging to a file. pymmcore-plus.log in the pymmcore-plus log directory PYMM_LOG_RICH Use rich for stderr logging (1, true or yes). Adds some formatting overhead (#449). "0" (disabled) MICROMANAGER_PATH Override location of Micro-Manager directory (with device adapters) Found automatically (see the search order) PYMM_SIGNALS_BACKEND The event backend to use. Must be one of 'qt', 'psygnal', or 'auto' auto (Qt if a QApplication exists when CMMCorePlus is created, otherwise psygnal) PYMM_DISABLE_IPYTHON_COMPLETIONS Set to 1 to disable Tab autocompletion for IPython "0" (enabled) UNICORE_SEQUENCE_BUFFER_MB Size of the sequence buffer used by UniMMCore for Python cameras, in MB. 1024 MB (250 MB on CI)

items.title: Micro-Manager Device Adapters
items.text: Just like the underlying pymmcore library, pymmcore-plus relies on the device adapters and C++ core provided by mmCoreAndDevices. (The Python packages themselves are covered on the Installation page.)

items.title: Installing Micro-Manager device adapters
items.text:
The device adapters can be installed in two ways:

  1. Use the mmcore command line tool

    pymmcore-plus provides a quick way to install the latest compatible version of Micro-Manager:

    mmcore install

    This will download the most recent nightly build of Micro-Manager that matches your version of pymmcore and, by default, place it in a pymmcore-plus/mm folder in the user's data directory:

    OS Path Windows C:\Users\UserName\AppData\Local\pymmcore-plus\pymmcore-plus\mm macOS ~/Library/Application Support/pymmcore-plus/mm Linux ~/.local/share/pymmcore-plus/mm

    If you would like to modify the location of the installation, or the release of Micro-Manager to install, you can use the --dest and --release flags respectively.

    For more information on the install command, run:

    mmcore install --help

    To explore all the mmcore command line tool functionalities, run mmcore --help (or see the CLI reference).

  2. Download manually from micro-manager.org

    Go to the Micro-Manager nightly builds page and download a build for your operating system whose device interface version matches your pymmcore (see below). This is not necessarily the latest release.

Apple Silicon and Linux

Micro-Manager only publishes nightly builds for Windows and Intel macOS. On Linux, and on macOS with an Apple Silicon (M1, M2, ...) processor, mmcore install prints Unsupported platform/architecture for nightly build and installs just the test adapters (DemoCamera, Utilities, SequenceTester and NotificationTester) from mm-test-adapters. That's enough for the demo configuration used throughout these docs, but to control real hardware you will need to build the adapters you need (see Building device adapters below).

Critical

The device interface version MUST match between pymmcore and the Micro-Manager device adapters. See below.

items.title: Showing the current installation
items.text:
To see which Micro-Manager installations pymmcore-plus has found, and which one it is using, run:

mmcore list

The output looks something like this (the active installation is marked with ➤):

Required pymmcore device interface version: 75

📁 ~/Library/Application Support/pymmcore-plus/mm
   ➤ Micro-Manager-75.20260226 (DIV 75) (active)
   • Micro-Manager-74.20260129 (DIV 74) (incompatible)

From Python, you can use find_micromanager:

python -c "from pymmcore_plus import find_micromanager; print(find_micromanager())"

items.title: Setting the active installation
items.text:
When you create a CMMCorePlus, pymmcore-plus looks for device adapters in the following places, and uses the first one whose device interface version matches pymmcore:

  1. The MICROMANAGER_PATH environment variable (always used, if set).
  2. A path previously selected with mmcore use (see below). If it's no longer compatible, it is forgotten (with a warning).
  3. The mmcore install folder in the user data directory (see the table above). If there are several compatible installations there, the last one in alphabetical order is used.
  4. The mm-test-adapters Python package, if it is installed.
  5. A Micro-Manager* folder in the default Micro-Manager install location: C:\Program Files\ on Windows, /Applications/ on macOS, and /usr/local/lib/ on Linux.

So if you already have Micro-Manager installed in the default location, and mmcore list says that it is compatible, it will be found automatically (unless one of the earlier locations also has a compatible installation). If mmcore list says that it's incompatible, run mmcore install to get a compatible set of adapters.

Using the Micro-Manager app too?

That's fine, but pymmcore-plus doesn't connect to a running Micro-Manager (it loads the device adapters itself). Most devices can only be opened by one program at a time, so close Micro-Manager before you load the same hardware configuration in Python (and vice versa).

To override the device adapter search path for a single session (or script), set the MICROMANAGER_PATH environment variable:

export MICROMANAGER_PATH=/path/to/installation

(For a single core object, you can also pass the folder directly: CMMCorePlus(mm_path="/path/to/installation").)

If you want to permanently set the Micro-Manager installation path that pymmcore-plus uses, you can use the mmcore use command:

mmcore use <some path or pattern>

... where <some path or pattern> is either a path to an existing directory (containing Micro-Manager device adapters) or a pattern to match against directories returned by find_micromanager.

Alternatively, you can use the use_micromanager function, passing either a path to an existing directory, or a pattern to match against directories returned by find_micromanager:

python -c "from pymmcore_plus import use_micromanager; use_micromanager(path=..., pattern=...)"

items.title: Building device adapters
items.text:
On Linux and Apple Silicon there are no pre-built Micro-Manager adapters beyond the test devices, so you will need to build the C++ core and device adapters yourself from mmCoreAndDevices. To do that, follow the build instructions in the micro-manager repo, then point pymmcore-plus at the folder with mmcore use.

On macOS and Linux, mmcore build-dev can also clone the repository and build a few adapters for you (DemoCamera, Utilities and SequenceTester by default, or the names you pass it). Not all adapters will build this way, and you'll need the build tools described in the instructions above. Run mmcore build-dev --help for the options.

items.title: Understanding device interface versions
items.text:
Micro-Manager's C++ layer (called MMCore) controls devices via adapters that are compiled into platform-specific shared libraries. These libraries are always compiled to work with a specific "device interface version" expected by the MMCore object itself. If you try to load a device adapter with a device interface version that does not match the version expected by the core, then you will get an error.

pymmcore is a library that wraps the C++ code and makes it available to Python. It has a 5-number version string that looks something like 12.5.1.75.0. The first three parts (here: 12.5.1) represent the version of the MMCore library. The next number (here: 75) is the device interface version that pymmcore expects. (The last number is a pymmcore-specific build number). To query version information of your installed libraries you can run:

mmcore --version

Critical

You must use device adapter libraries that were compiled for the same device interface version as your version of pymmcore.

By default, when you run mmcore install, it will pick the latest compatible version to install. However, you can also do this explicitly. For example, with an older pymmcore that expects device interface version 74, you could explicitly install the last compatible device adapters listed on the table below with mmcore install as follows:

mmcore install -r 20260225

Here is a list of the latest device interface numbers, the date of the first nightly build where they were available, the last nightly build date to support that version, and the commit in mmCoreAndDevices that bumped the version.
