        """Called when device is initialized."""
        # Setup hardware connections, configure device, etc.
        self.connect_to_hardware()
        super().initialize()  # Call parent if needed

items.title: 3. Usage
items.text:
Once loaded and initialized, use the device through the standard CMMCore API:

# Set as current device
core.setCameraDevice("Camera1")

# Use standard API
core.setExposure(50)
image = core.snap()

items.title: 4. Shutdown
items.text:
# Shutdown specific device
core.unloadDevice("Camera1")

# Or shutdown all devices
core.unloadAllDevices()

Override shutdown() for cleanup:

class MyCamera(CameraDevice):
    def shutdown(self) -> None:
        """Called when device is unloaded."""
        self.disconnect_from_hardware()
        super().shutdown()

items.title: Thread safety
items.text:
When the core calls into a Python device, it does so with the device locked, so those calls don't run concurrently.

If you need manual locking:

device = MyCamera()
core.loadPyDevice("Camera", device)

# Manual locking
with device:
    # Device is locked for this block
    device.some_internal_method()

items.title: Events and metadata
items.text:
You can connect to the events of a UniMMCore as usual, but note that it doesn't (yet) emit propertyChanged when you set a property on a Python device, or exposureChanged for a Python camera (state devices are the exception). Until it does, a device can emit events itself, through its core attribute:

class MyDevice(GenericDevice):
    _level = 1

    @pymm_property(limits=(0, 10))
    def level(self) -> int:
        return self._level

    @level.setter
    def level(self, value: int) -> None:
        self._level = value
        self.core.events.propertyChanged.emit(self.get_label(), "level", str(value))

(Please open an issue if this matters for your device.)

Sequence acquisitions include metadata just as C++ camera adapters do:

core.startSequenceAcquisition(10, 0, True)
while core.isSequenceRunning() or core.getRemainingImageCount():
    if core.getRemainingImageCount():
        img, metadata = core.popNextImageAndMD()
        print(f"Image {metadata['ImageNumber']}: {metadata['ElapsedTime-ms']} ms")

(The metadata contains the standard keys, like ImageNumber, ElapsedTime-ms, Camera, Width and Height, plus whatever your start_sequence yielded.)

items.title: Error handling
items.text:
Exceptions raised in Python devices propagate to the caller:

class MyCamera(CameraDevice):
    def set_exposure(self, exposure: float) -> None:
        if exposure < 0:
            raise ValueError("Exposure must be positive")
        if exposure > 10000:
            raise ValueError("Exposure too long")
        self._exposure = exposure

core.setExposure(-5)  # raises ValueError: Exposure must be positive

items.title: Python devices in config files
items.text:
UniMMCore can load and save Python devices in regular Micro-Manager .cfg files. Python device lines are prefixed with #py, so a regular CMMCorePlus (or Micro-Manager itself) reads them as comments and ignores them:

# C++ devices
Device,Camera,DemoCamera,DCam

# Python devices: pyDevice,<label>,<module>,<class>
#py pyDevice,PyCamera,my_devices,MyCamera
#py Property,Core,Camera,PyCamera

The module must be importable (e.g. installed, or on sys.path) when the file is loaded with core.loadSystemConfiguration("my.cfg"). To write the current state (C++ and Python devices) to a file, use core.saveSystemConfiguration("my.cfg"). Pass prefix_py_devices=False to write the Python lines without the #py prefix (the file can then only be loaded by UniMMCore).

items.title: Complete examples
items.text:
For complete working examples, see these scripts in the examples/ folder of the repository:

  • unicore_camera.py: a synthetic camera with temporal patterns
  • unicore_hamamatsu.py: a real Hamamatsu camera
  • unicore.py: a basic XY stage with properties

items.title: Events
items.text:
There are two objects that emit events in pymmcore-plus. The CMMCorePlus object emits the PCoreSignaler signals at core.events when the state of the microscope changes, and the MDARunner emits the PMDASignaler signals at core.mda.events as an acquisition sequence progresses.

See Events and Callbacks for how to connect callbacks, choosing the Qt or psygnal backend, and which thread your callbacks run on.

items.title: PCoreSignaler
items.text:
Bases: Protocol

Declares the protocol for all signals that will be emitted from CMMCorePlus.

The main instance of this interface is available on the CMMCorePlus object at the events attribute. Each signal on events is an object that has a connect and a disconnect method that you can use to connect/disconnect your own callback functions. connect and disconnect accept a single argument, which is a callable that will be called when the signal is emitted. The callable should accept no more positional arguments than the signal emits (noted for each signal below), but may accept fewer.

Note

These events are a superset of those emitted by MMEventCallback in the MMCore C++ library. The "on" prefix has been removed from the names here and the first letter lower cased.

Important

In the core C++ library (and in pymmcore), the emission of many of these events is left to the discretion of the device adapter. In pymmcore_plus, we attempt to emit these events in a more consistent manner (e.g. by checking a particular value before and after calling into the C++ library). So, the emission of these events is not guaranteed to be 1:1 with the C++ library; however, it should be easier to follow the state of the core when using pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus.

Examples:

To connect to the onExposureChanged event emitted by MMCore, you would connect to the exposureChanged signal on this class:

from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()


def on_exposure_changed(device: str, new_exposure: float):
    print(f"Exposure changed for {device} to {new_exposure}")


core.events.exposureChanged.connect(on_exposure_changed)

Events may also be connected as a decorator:

@core.events.exposureChanged.connect
def on_exposure_changed(device: str, new_exposure: float): ...

items.title: pymmcore-widgets
items.text:
pymmcore-widgets is a library of Qt widgets for pymmcore-plus, meant for building your own microscope GUI in Python. There are widgets for most of the things you do at the microscope (channels, exposure, stages, device properties, configuration groups, snapping and live mode, multi-dimensional acquisitions) and for setting it up (the Hardware Configuration Wizard, pixel sizes, installing device adapters). Most of them control a CMMCorePlus and follow its events, so they stay in sync with each other and with your own code. They are also the building blocks of pymmcore-gui and napari-micromanager.

A few widgets in one window (the code is the StageExplorer example).

items.title: Where to start
items.text:
• Your first GUI puts a few of them together in a window.
  • The widget gallery shows each widget with a screenshot, and links to its page with a runnable example and the API.
  • Building a custom GUI covers choosing a Qt backend, how widgets find their core, and a larger example.
  • Qt integration explains how pymmcore-plus and Qt work together (and how to keep your GUI responsive).

items.title: API reference
items.text:
Import widgets from the top-level package:

from pymmcore_widgets import MDAWidget, PropertyBrowser, StageWidget

Each of these has its own page (listed under pymmcore_widgets in the sidebar, and in the gallery). A few more specialized widgets live in submodules: the sequence editors' building blocks in pymmcore_widgets.useq_widgets (for example WellPlateWidget and PointsPlanWidget), and StackViewer in pymmcore_widgets.experimental.

items.title: Contributing to pymmcore-widgets
items.text:
Thanks for thinking of a way to help improve this library!

Remember that contributions come in all shapes and sizes beyond writing bug fixes. Contributing to documentation, opening new issues for bugs, asking for clarification on things you find unclear or requesting new features, are all super valuable contributions.

You can do any of the above by opening a new issue or by submitting a pull request on the GitHub repository for this project. The contributing guide has the parts that are the same for every package (and the ways to reach us); this page has the parts that are specific to the widgets.

items.title: Development setup
items.text:
We use uv. uv sync installs the package with its dev dependency group, which includes PyQt6:

git clone <your-fork>
cd pymmcore-widgets
uv sync
uv run mmcore install  # the demo device adapters, used by most tests

items.title: Running the tests
items.text:
uv run pytest

Some of the tests show real windows. To run them without any windows (on a machine without a display, or just to keep your screen quiet), use Qt's offscreen platform:

QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen uv run pytest

(On Windows PowerShell: $env:QT_QPA_PLATFORM = "offscreen" first.) CI runs the tests on macOS and Windows, with both PyQt6 and PySide6.

items.title: Widget pages and screenshots
items.text:
Each widget's documentation page, its screenshots and its card in the widget gallery are generated by docs/_gen.py:

  • docs/widget_list.json lists the widgets, by gallery section.
  • examples/<snake_case_name>.py is the example for each one (e.g. examples/mda_widget.py for MDAWidget). _gen.py runs it offscreen, grabs the window it shows (in light and dark mode), and puts the code on the widget's page.
  • The widget's docstring becomes the rest of the page, and its first line is the description on the gallery card.

So, to add a widget to the docs, export it from pymmcore_widgets, add it to widget_list.json, and write an example that shows it with the demo configuration. _gen.py warns about exported widgets that are missing from the list. You can run it yourself to check that the example works:

uv run python docs/_gen.py          # only redoes screenshots whose example changed
uv run python docs/_gen.py --force  # redo them all

The output (docs/api/, docs/_generated/, docs/images/generated/) is not committed. The docs themselves are built as part of the unified pymmcore-plus site: see How These Docs Work to preview them.

items.title: Building a Custom GUI
items.text: The widgets in pymmcore-widgets are ordinary QWidgets that control a CMMCorePlus, so you can arrange them with Qt layouts like any other widget. Your first GUI puts a few of them in a window. This page covers the things you'll want to know once you start building something bigger: which Qt to install, how widgets find their core, and a larger example.

items.title: Installing a Qt backend
items.text:
pymmcore-widgets does not install Qt for you, so you choose the Qt backend with an extra:

pip install "pymmcore-widgets[PyQt6]"
# or
pip install "pymmcore-widgets[PySide6]"

(Keep the quotes. In zsh, the default shell on macOS, the square brackets otherwise cause a "no matches found" error.) You'll also need Python 3.11 or newer, and the Micro-Manager device adapters (see Installation).

PyQt6 or PySide6?

Qt is the C++ toolkit the widgets are drawn with, and PyQt6 and PySide6 are two sets of Python bindings for it. The widgets work with (and are tested on) both, on macOS and Windows. The main difference is the license. PyQt6 is GPL (or commercial), and PySide6 is LGPL. That matters if you distribute your GUI, for example as a bundled application. If you don't have a reason to choose, PyQt6 is a fine default (it's what pymmcore-gui uses).

We no longer test PyQt5 or PySide2 (and PySide2 can't be installed on Python 3.11 or newer).

The widgets import Qt through qtpy, which is installed with pymmcore-widgets. qtpy provides one API (from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication) on top of whichever binding is installed, and the examples on this site use it too. If you write your own code against qtpy as well, it will run with either backend. (If both are installed in the same environment, qtpy picks PyQt6; set the environment variable QT_API=pyside6 to use PySide6.)

items.title: Basic usage
items.text:
For a basic use of any of the widgets, we need to:

  1. create a Qt application (QApplication);
  2. create a Micro-Manager core instance so that all the widgets will control the same core;
  3. load a configuration file;
  4. create and show the widget(s) we want.

The order of the first two steps matters. Create the QApplication before the core (see Qt integration for why).

In this example, we replace step 3 with the ConfigurationWidget, which lets us load any Micro-Manager configuration file. We also add the GroupPresetTableWidget, which shows the configuration groups and presets stored in the configuration file:

basic_usage.py
# import the necessary packages
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

from pymmcore_widgets import ConfigurationWidget, GroupPresetTableWidget

# create a QApplication
app = QApplication([])

# create a CMMCorePlus instance.
mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance()

# create a ConfigurationWidget
cfg_widget = ConfigurationWidget()

# create a GroupPresetTableWidget
gp_widget = GroupPresetTableWidget()

# show the created widgets
cfg_widget.show()
gp_widget.show()

app.exec()

The code above will create a Qt application with the ConfigurationWidget and the GroupPresetTableWidget:

items.title: Choosing a core
items.text:
By default, most widgets use the global singleton core, CMMCorePlus.instance(), and create it if it doesn't exist yet. This means that all the widgets in your GUI control the same core without you connecting anything, and so does any other code that calls CMMCorePlus.instance(). (So in the example above, the mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance() line isn't strictly necessary. Without it, the ConfigurationWidget would create the core.)

If you need a specific core instead, create it first and pass it to each widget as the mmcore argument, for example GroupPresetTableWidget(mmcore=my_core). A few widgets are different:

  • The sequence editors (MDASequenceWidget, ChannelTable, PositionTable, TimePlanWidget, ZPlanWidget and GridPlanWidget) don't use a core at all. They edit useq objects. Read the result with value(), set it with setValue(), and connect to valueChanged. MDAWidget is the sequence editor that is connected to a core (and can run the acquisition).
  • ConfigWizard calls the argument core, not mmcore.
  • ConfigGroupsEditor and ConfigGroupsTree are built from a core with create_from_core(core), and don't follow it afterwards.
  • InstallWidget installs device adapters and doesn't need a core.

items.title: Custom GUI
items.text:
The widgets are ordinary QWidgets, so building a custom GUI with them is mostly a matter of Qt layouts. If you're new to Qt, the Qt for Python tutorials are a good place to start. Here, we only give a simple example of a custom GUI built from some of the pymmcore-widgets.

We create a Qt application with a general-purpose QWidget that incorporates a variety of pymmcore-widgets: ConfigurationWidget, ChannelGroupWidget, ChannelWidget, DefaultCameraExposureWidget, ImagePreview, SnapButton, and LiveButton.

This simple GUI can be used to load a Micro-Manager configuration file, snap an image or stream images from the camera, with the flexibility to select a channel and adjust the exposure time:

custom_gui.py
# Import the necessary packages
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QGridLayout, QWidget

from pymmcore_widgets import (
    ChannelGroupWidget,
    ChannelWidget,
    ConfigurationWidget,
    DefaultCameraExposureWidget,
    ImagePreview,
    LiveButton,
    SnapButton,
)


# Create a QWidget class named MyWidget
class MyWidget(QWidget):
    """An example QWidget that uses some of the widgets in pymmcore_widgets."""

    def __init__(self, parent: QWidget | None = None):
        super().__init__(parent=parent)

        # This is not strictly necessary but we can create a Micro-Manager core
        # instance so that all the widgets can control the same core. If you don't
        # create a core instance, the first widget to be instantiated will create
        # a new core instance.
        CMMCorePlus.instance()

        # Create the wanted pymmcore_widgets
        cfg = ConfigurationWidget()
        ch_group_combo = ChannelGroupWidget()
        ch_combo = ChannelWidget()
        exp = DefaultCameraExposureWidget()
        preview = ImagePreview()
        snap = SnapButton()
        live = LiveButton()

        # Create the layout for MyWidget
        # In Qt, a `layout` (https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/layout.html) is used to add
        # widgets to a `QWidget`. For this example, we'll employ a
        # `QGridLayout` (https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qgridlayout.html) to organize the
        # widgets in a grid-like arrangement.
        layout = QGridLayout(self)

        # Add the wanted pymmcore_widgets to the layout.
        # The first two arguments of 'addWidget' specify the grid position
        # in terms of rows and columns. The third and fourth arguments
        # define the span of the widget across multiple rows and columns.
        layout.addWidget(cfg, 0, 0, 1, 3)
        layout.addWidget(ch_group_combo, 1, 0)
        layout.addWidget(ch_combo, 1, 1)
        layout.addWidget(exp, 1, 2)
        layout.addWidget(preview, 2, 0, 1, 3)
        layout.addWidget(snap, 3, 1)
        layout.addWidget(live, 3, 2)


# Create a QApplication and show MyWidget
if __name__ == "__main__":
    from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

    app = QApplication([])
    widget = MyWidget()
    widget.show()
    app.exec()

Running it (and loading a configuration) looks like this:

items.title: Next steps
items.text: The widget gallery lists the other widgets you can add, each with an example. If you'd rather start from a ready-made application, see pymmcore-gui (which you can also extend with your own widgets) or napari-micromanager.

items.title: Troubleshooting Qt and Widgets
items.text: For problems with the core itself (finding Micro-Manager, loading device adapters), see Troubleshooting for pymmcore-plus.

items.title: No Qt bindings
items.text:
qtpy.QtBindingsNotFoundError: No Qt bindings could be found

If you get an error similar to the one above, it means that you did not install one of the necessary PyQt or PySide libraries. Install pymmcore-widgets with an extra that brings one along:

pip install "pymmcore-widgets[PyQt6]"  # or "pymmcore-widgets[PySide6]"

See Installing a Qt backend for how to choose.

items.title: "no matches found" when installing
items.text:
zsh: no matches found: pymmcore-widgets[PyQt6]

zsh (the default shell on macOS) treats the square brackets as a file pattern. Put quotes around the package name: pip install "pymmcore-widgets[PyQt6]".

items.title: Must construct a QApplication
items.text:
QWidget: Must construct a QApplication before a QWidget

... followed by Python crashing. Every Qt program needs a QApplication, and it must exist before you create any widget. Create it first thing (and create it before the CMMCorePlus, too, for the reasons explained in Qt integration):

from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

app = QApplication([])
# ... now create the core and the widgets
app.exec()

items.title: The widgets don't follow my script
items.text:
If you change something from your own code (core.setExposure(50), say) and a widget doesn't update, the widget is probably connected to a different core. Widgets use the global CMMCorePlus.instance() unless you pass mmcore=, so a core you created with CMMCorePlus() is a separate object, with its own devices and its own events. Either use CMMCorePlus.instance() in your script, or pass your core to each widget: ExposureWidget(mmcore=my_core).

Also check that the widget uses a core at all (the sequence editors, like ChannelTable and ZPlanWidget, don't). See Choosing a core.

items.title: The GUI freezes
items.text:
Anything that blocks the main thread (the one running app.exec()) freezes the whole GUI until it returns: a long core.snapImage(), a slow stage move, a time.sleep() in a callback, etc... Run long operations in a thread instead. CMMCorePlus.run_mda already does this for you. See Qt integration for an example.

Please open an issue if you run into something that isn't covered here.

"""Example usage of the ChannelTable class.

ChannelTable edits a list of `useq.Channel`s.  It doesn't use a CMMCorePlus, so
you tell it which channel groups and channels to offer.

Check also the 'mda_widget.py' example to see the ChannelTable

"""

from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

examples/config_groups_editor.py
"""ConfigGroupsEditor edits configuration groups and their presets.

It doesn't change the core: when you click "Apply", it emits `applyRequested`
with the changes, and it's up to you what to do with them.
"""

from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

from pymmcore_widgets import ConfigGroupsEditor

app = QApplication([])
core = CMMCorePlus.instance()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()

# load the core's devices, groups and presets into the editor
# (pass `load_configs=False` to start with an empty list of groups)
cfg = ConfigGroupsEditor.create_from_core(core)


# connect to apply signal to print the changes
def _on_apply_clicked(changed, deleted, channel_group):
    print("\n\nApply clicked:")
    print(f"Changed: {[cg.name for cg in changed]}")
    print(f"Deleted: {deleted}")
    print(f"Channel group: {channel_group}")


cfg.applyRequested.connect(_on_apply_clicked)

cfg.resize(900, 550)
cfg.show()

app.exec()

"""ImagePreview shows the latest image from the core (snapped or live).

Here it's combined with a few other widgets into a minimal "snap and live" window.
"""

from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication, QGroupBox, QHBoxLayout, QVBoxLayout, QWidget

from pymmcore_widgets import (
    ChannelWidget,
    ExposureWidget,
    ImagePreview,
    LiveButton,
    SnapButton,
)


class ImageFrame(QWidget):
    """An example widget with a snap/live button and an image preview."""

    def __init__(self, parent: QWidget | None = None) -> None:
        super().__init__(parent)

        self.preview = ImagePreview()
        self.snap_button = SnapButton()
        self.live_button = LiveButton()
        self.exposure = ExposureWidget()
        self.channel = ChannelWidget()

        self.setLayout(QVBoxLayout())

        buttons = QGroupBox()
        buttons.setLayout(QHBoxLayout())
        buttons.layout().addWidget(self.snap_button)
        buttons.layout().addWidget(self.live_button)

        ch_exp = QWidget()
        layout = QHBoxLayout()
        layout.setContentsMargins(0, 0, 0, 0)
        ch_exp.setLayout(layout)

        ch = QGroupBox()
        ch.setTitle("Channel")
        ch.setLayout(QHBoxLayout())
        ch.layout().setContentsMargins(0, 0, 0, 0)
        ch.layout().addWidget(self.channel)
        layout.addWidget(ch)

        exp = QGroupBox()
        exp.setTitle("Exposure")
        exp.setLayout(QHBoxLayout())
        exp.layout().setContentsMargins(0, 0, 0, 0)
        exp.layout().addWidget(self.exposure)
        layout.addWidget(exp)

        self.layout().addWidget(self.preview)
        self.layout().addWidget(ch_exp)
        self.layout().addWidget(buttons)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app = QApplication([])
    mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance()
    mmc.loadSystemConfiguration()
    frame = ImageFrame()
    frame.show()
    mmc.snap()
    app.exec()

"""MDAWidget is a widget for creating and running a useq.MDASequence.

get_next_available_path(requested_path: Path) -> Path

Get the next available path.

This method is called immediately before running an MDA to ensure that the file being saved does not overwrite an existing file. It is also called at the end of the experiment to update the save widget with the next available path.

It may be overridden to provide custom behavior, but it should always return a Path object to a non-existing file or folder.

The default behavior adds/increments a 3-digit counter at the end of the path (before the extension) if the path already exists.

"""Example usage of the ShuttersWidget class.

In this example all the devices of type 'Shutter' that are loaded
in the core are displayed with a 'ShuttersWidget'.

The autoshutter checkbox is displayed only with the last shutter device.
"""

from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus, DeviceType
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication, QHBoxLayout, QWidget

from pymmcore_widgets import ShuttersWidget

app = QApplication([])

mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance()
mmc.loadSystemConfiguration()

wdg = QWidget()
wdg.setLayout(QHBoxLayout())

shutter_dev_list = list(mmc.getLoadedDevicesOfType(DeviceType.Shutter))

for idx, shutter_dev in enumerate(shutter_dev_list):
    # bool to display the autoshutter checkbox only with the last shutter
    autoshutter = bool(idx >= len(shutter_dev_list) - 1)
    shutter = ShuttersWidget(
        shutter_dev,
        autoshutter=autoshutter,
        # label the button with the device name
        button_text_open=shutter_dev,
        button_text_closed=shutter_dev,
    )
    wdg.layout().addWidget(shutter)

wdg.show()

app.exec()

from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
from qtpy.QtCore import QModelIndex
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication, QHBoxLayout, QSplitter, QVBoxLayout, QWidget

from pymmcore_widgets import (
    CameraRoiWidget,
    GroupPresetTableWidget,
    MDAWidget,
    StageExplorer,
    StageWidget,
)

app = QApplication([])

mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance()
mmc.loadSystemConfiguration()
mmc.setProperty("Camera", "BitDepth", "12")

# set camera roi (rectangular helps confirm orientation)
mmc.setROI(0, 0, 600, 400)

xy = mmc.getXYStageDevice()
if mmc.hasProperty(xy, "Velocity"):
    mmc.setProperty(xy, "Velocity", 2)

explorer = StageExplorer()
stage_ctrl = StageWidget(mmc.getXYStageDevice())
stage_ctrl.setStep(512)
stage_ctrl.snap_checkbox.setChecked(True)

z_ctrl = StageWidget(mmc.getFocusDevice())
z_ctrl.snap_checkbox.setChecked(True)

mda_widget = MDAWidget()
group_wdg = GroupPresetTableWidget()
cam_roi = CameraRoiWidget()


# As an example...
# When ROIs are edited or destroyed, update the MDA widget's stage positions.
def _on_data_changed(top_left: QModelIndex, bottom_right: QModelIndex) -> None:
    mgr = explorer.roi_manager
    positions = [
        roi.create_useq_position(overlap=mgr.scan_overlap, mode=mgr.scan_mode)
        for roi in mgr.all_rois()
    ]
    # optional: skip positions that don't actually have a valid sequence (grid plan)
    positions = [pos for pos in positions if pos.sequence is not None]
    mda_widget.stage_positions.setValue(positions)


model = explorer.roi_manager.roi_model
model.dataChanged.connect(_on_data_changed)
model.rowsRemoved.connect(_on_data_changed)


# layout

splitter = QSplitter()
left = QWidget()
llayout = QVBoxLayout(left)
llayout.addWidget(group_wdg)
llayout.addWidget(cam_roi)
splitter.addWidget(left)
splitter.addWidget(explorer)
right = QWidget()
rlayout = QVBoxLayout(right)
rtop = QHBoxLayout()
rtop.addWidget(stage_ctrl)
rtop.addWidget(z_ctrl)
rlayout.addLayout(rtop)
rlayout.addWidget(mda_widget)
splitter.addWidget(right)
splitter.show()

app.exec()

items.title: Example
items.text:
examples/stage_widget.py
"""Example usage of the StageWidget class.

In this example all the devices of type 'Stage' and 'XYStage' that are loaded
in micromanager are displayed with a 'StageWidget'.
"""

from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus, DeviceType
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication, QGroupBox, QHBoxLayout, QWidget

from pymmcore_widgets import StageWidget

app = QApplication([])

mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance()
mmc.loadSystemConfiguration()

wdg = QWidget()
wdg_layout = QHBoxLayout(wdg)

stages = list(mmc.getLoadedDevicesOfType(DeviceType.XYStage))
stages.extend(mmc.getLoadedDevicesOfType(DeviceType.Stage))
for stage in stages:
    lbl = "Z" if mmc.getDeviceType(stage) == DeviceType.Stage else "XY"
    bx = QGroupBox(f"{lbl} Control")
    bx_layout = QHBoxLayout(bx)
    bx_layout.setContentsMargins(0, 0, 0, 0)
    bx_layout.addWidget(StageWidget(device=stage, position_label_below=True))
    wdg_layout.addWidget(bx)


wdg.show()
app.exec()

items.title: filterDevices
items.text:
filterDevices(
    query: str | Pattern = "",
    *,
    exclude_devices: Iterable[DeviceType] = (),
    include_devices: Iterable[DeviceType] = (),
    include_read_only: bool = True,
    include_pre_init: bool = True,
    always_show_checked: bool = False,
    predicate: Callable[[DeviceProperty], bool | None] | None = None,
) -> None

Update the table to only show devices that match the given query/filter.

Filters are applied in the following order: 1. If include_devices is provided, only devices of the specified types will be considered. 2. If exclude_devices is provided, devices of the specified types will be hidden (even if they are in include_devices). 3. If always_show_checked is True, remaining rows that are checked will always be shown, regardless of other filters. 4. If predicate is provided and it returns False, the row is hidden. 5. If include_read_only is False, read-only properties are hidden. 6. If include_pre_init is False, pre-initialized properties are hidden. 7. Query filtering is applied last, hiding rows that do not match the query.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default query str | Pattern

A string or regex pattern to match against the device-property names. If empty, no filtering is applied, by default ""

'' exclude_devices Iterable[DeviceType]

A list of device types to exclude from the table, by default ()

() include_devices Iterable[DeviceType]

A list of device types to include in the table, by default ()

() include_read_only bool

Whether to include read-only properties in the table, by default True

True include_pre_init bool

Whether to include pre-initialized properties in the table, by default True

True always_show_checked bool

Whether to always include rows that are checked, by default False.

False predicate Callable[[DeviceProperty, QTableWidgetItem], bool | None] | None

A function that takes a DeviceProperty and QTableWidgetItem and returns True to include the row, False to exclude it, or None to skip filtering. If None, no additional filtering is applied, by default None

items.title: Widget Gallery
items.text:
The top-level widgets in pymmcore-widgets, grouped by what they do, roughly in the order you'd reach for them when building a GUI. Click a widget for a runnable example and its API (the screenshots are generated from those examples).

Most of these widgets control a CMMCorePlus (by default the global CMMCorePlus.instance(), or the one you pass as mmcore=). They follow the core's events, so they stay in sync with each other and with your own code. The sequence editors are the exception: they don't use a core at all. (See Building a custom GUI for the details.)

items.title: Camera and images
items.text:
Snap and live buttons, an image preview, and the camera's exposure and ROI.

  • SnapButton

    Button that snaps an image with the current camera.

  • LiveButton

    Button that starts and stops live mode.

  • ImagePreview

    A Widget that displays the latest image from the core.

  • ExposureWidget

    Spin box that shows and sets the exposure time (in ms) of a camera.

  • DefaultCameraExposureWidget

    A Widget to get/set exposure on the default camera.

  • CameraRoiWidget

    A Widget to control the camera device ROI.

items.title: Channels, objectives and presets
items.text:
These widgets show (and change) the current state of the microscope: the channel, the objective, the preset of any configuration group, and the shutters.

  • ChannelWidget

    Combo box that shows and sets the current channel.

  • ChannelGroupWidget

    Combo box that chooses which configuration group is the channel group.

  • ObjectivesWidget

    Combo box that shows and sets the current objective.

  • PresetsWidget

    Combo box that shows and sets the current preset of one configuration group.

  • GroupPresetTableWidget

    Table of all configuration groups, to view and set their presets.

  • ShuttersWidget

    Button that opens and closes a shutter, with an optional autoshutter checkbox.

items.title: Stages
items.text:
Move an XY or Z stage, or explore the sample in a zoomable view of the stage, where snapped images appear at the position they were taken.

  • StageWidget

    Arrow buttons to move an XY stage or a Z (focus) stage.

  • StageExplorer

    Zoomable view of the stage, where snapped images appear at their positions.

items.title: Devices and properties
items.text:
View and change the properties of any of the loaded devices.

  • PropertyBrowser

    A Widget to browse and change properties of all devices.

  • PropertiesWidget

    Controls for a filtered set of device properties (a PropertyWidget each).

  • PropertyWidget

    Widget to display and control a single device property.

items.title: Acquisition
items.text:
Define a multi-dimensional acquisition (a useq.MDASequence) and run it on the core. MDAWidget is the MDASequenceWidget below, connected to a core. It offers the core's channels, can add the current stage position, and has buttons to run, pause and cancel the acquisition.

  • MDAWidget

    Main MDA Widget connected to a pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus instance.

  • HCSWizard

    A wizard to set up a high-content screening (HCS) experiment.

items.title: Sequence editors
items.text:
No core needed

These widgets edit useq objects and don't touch the microscope. Read the result with value(), set it with setValue(), and connect to valueChanged to hear about changes. Use them to describe an experiment in your own GUI; to run one, pass the sequence to CMMCorePlus.run_mda (or use the MDAWidget above).

  • MDASequenceWidget

    A widget that provides a GUI to construct and edit a useq.MDASequence.

  • ChannelTable

    Table to edit a list of channels (useq.Channel).

  • TimePlanWidget

    Table to edit a time plan (useq.AnyTimePlan), one row per phase.

  • ZPlanWidget

    Widget to edit a z plan (useq.AnyZPlan).

  • PositionTable

    Table to edit a list of stage positions (useq.Position).

  • GridPlanWidget

    Widget to edit a grid plan.

items.title: Configuration and setup
items.text:
Load, create and edit a configuration file (the ConfigWizard is Micro-Manager's Hardware Configuration Wizard), set pixel sizes, install device adapters, and watch the core's log.

  • ConfigurationWidget

    A Widget to select and load a Micro-Manager system configuration.

  • ConfigWizard

    Hardware Configuration Wizard for Micro-Manager.

  • ConfigGroupsEditor

    Editor for configuration groups and their presets.

  • ConfigGroupsTree

    A tree widget that displays configuration groups.

  • PixelConfigurationWidget

    A Widget to define the pixel size configurations.

  • ObjectivesPixelConfigurationWidget

    A Widget to define the pixel size configurations using the objective device.

  • InstallWidget

    Widget to install Micro-Manager's device adapters (like mmcore install).

  • CoreLogWidget

    Live view of the core's log file.

items.title: useq-schema
items.text:
useq-schema (imported as useq) is an implementation-agnostic schema for describing a sequence of events during a multi-dimensional imaging acquisition: the time points, stage positions, channels, z-planes, etc... that you want to acquire. It describes what to do, and leaves it to an acquisition engine (such as the one in pymmcore-plus) to actually do it.

The goal of useq-schema is to provide a specification (and some python utilities) for generating event objects that can be consumed by microscope acquisition engines. A hope is that this will encourage inter-operability between various efforts to drive automated image acquisition.

The schema tries to remain agnostic to the specific acquisition engine (though it was designed based on the capabilities of Micro-Manager). We welcome feedback from interested parties regarding limitations and/or potential extensions to the schema! Similarly, while the "ideal" schema will support arbitrary dimensions (i.e. more than the conventional position, time, channel, z, ...), it is also hard to avoid hard-coding some assumptions about dimensionality in certain places. Any and all feedback (even minor stuff, such as parameter naming, etc...) is welcome! Please open an issue.

items.title: A quick example
items.text:
from useq import MDASequence

mda_seq = MDASequence(
    stage_positions=[(100, 100, 30), (200, 150, 35)],
    channels=["DAPI", "FITC"],
    time_plan={"interval": 1, "loops": 20},
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 0.5},
    axis_order="tpcz",
)

The MDASequence object is iterable, yielding MDAEvent objects in the order specified by the axis_order attribute:

>>> mda_seq.sizes
{'t': 20, 'p': 2, 'c': 2, 'z': 9}
>>> events = list(mda_seq)
>>> len(events)
720
>>> events[1]
MDAEvent(index={'t': 0, 'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 1}, channel=Channel(config='DAPI'), min_start_time=0.0, x_pos=100.0, y_pos=100.0, z_pos=28.5)

Building Sequences walks through the common cases (time series, z-stacks, grids, skipping channels, etc...).

items.title: MDAEvent
items.text:
The primary "event" object is useq.MDAEvent. This describes a single event that a microscope should perform, including preparation of the hardware, and execution of the event (such as an image acquisition).

  • For Micro-Manager, this object is most similar (though not identical) to the events generated by generate-acq-sequence in the clojure acquisition engine that drives Micro-Manager's multi-dimensional acquisitions.
  • For Pycro-Manager, this object is similar to an individual acquisition event dict generated by multi_d_acquisition_events, (and, useq.pycromanager provides a to_pycromanager function that returns a dict following the pycro-manager event spec)

items.title: MDASequence
items.text:
useq.MDASequence represents a sequence of events, as might be generated by the multidimensional acquisition GUI in most microscope software. The Python MDASequence object is itself iterable, and yields useq.MDAEvent objects.

  • For Micro-Manager, this object is most similar to org.micromanager.acquisition.SequenceSettings, (generated by clicking the Acquire! button in the Multi-D Acquisition GUI)
  • For Pycro-Manager, this object is similar to the multi_d_acquisition_events convenience function, (and useq.pycromanager provides a to_pycromanager function that returns a list of pycro-manager event dicts)

items.title: Executing an MDASequence
items.text:
This library is just a schema, and does not provide any built-in functionality for executing an MDASequence. However, pymmcore-plus implements an acquisition engine that can execute an MDASequence object (or any iterable of MDAEvent objects) with Micro-Manager (via the pymmcore python wrapper around the C++ MMCore). The MDAWidget in pymmcore-widgets, pymmcore-gui and napari-micromanager all build a useq.MDASequence from user input and hand it to pymmcore-plus to run.

Built an engine that runs an MDASequence (or know of a similar schema in other software)? Open an issue and we'll list it here.

items.title: Serialization and deserialization
items.text:
MDASequence and MDAEvent objects are designed to be serialized and deserialized, allowing you to define an entire multi-dimensional acquisition in a human-readable YAML (or JSON) file, and then load that file into your acquisition engine.

For example, the following file defines an experiment with:

  • 3 channels (Cy5, FITC, and DAPI), specifying exposure times in ms for Cy5 and FITC, and acquiring DAPI (without a z-stack) only every third timepoint
  • a two-phase time-lapse: 3 frames, 3 seconds apart, followed by a frame every 10 seconds for 40 minutes
  • a Z-stack at each timepoint, with a range of 4 microns and a step size of 0.5 micron
  • two stage positions, specifying a unique Z-stack for the second position

Example

YAMLJSON my_experiment.yaml
axis_order: tpcz
channels:
  - config: Cy5
    exposure: 50.0
  - config: FITC
    exposure: 100.0
  - config: DAPI
    acquire_every: 3
    do_stack: false
time_plan:
  phases:
    - interval: 0:00:03
      loops: 3
    - duration: 0:40:00
      interval: 0:00:10
z_plan:
  range: 4.0
  step: 0.5
stage_positions:
  - x: 10.0
    y: 20.0
    z: 50.0
  - name: Cell 1
    x: 110.0
    y: 220.0
    z: 50.0
    sequence:
      z_plan:
        above: 10.0
        below: 0.0
        step: 1.0
metadata:
  some info: about my experiment
my_experiment.json
{
  "axis_order": "tpcz",
  "channels": [
    {
      "config": "Cy5",
      "exposure": 50.0
    },
    {
      "config": "FITC",
      "exposure": 100.0
    },
    {
      "config": "DAPI",
      "acquire_every": 3,
      "do_stack": false
    }
  ],
  "time_plan": {
    "phases": [
      {
        "interval": "0:00:03",
        "loops": 3
      },
      {
        "duration": "0:40:00",
        "interval": "0:00:10"
      }
    ]
  },
  "z_plan": {
    "range": 4.0,
    "step": 0.5
  },
  "stage_positions": [
    {
      "x": 10.0,
      "y": 20.0,
      "z": 50.0
    },
    {
      "name": "Cell 1",
      "x": 110.0,
      "y": 220.0,
      "z": 50.0,
      "sequence": {
        "z_plan": {
          "above": 10.0,
          "below": 0.0,
          "step": 1.0
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "metadata": {
    "some info": "about my experiment"
  }
}

Either file can be loaded with:

import useq

seq = useq.MDASequence.from_file("my_experiment.yaml")

... and seq.yaml() or seq.model_dump_json(exclude_unset=True) go the other way (see saving and loading sequences).

Unknown keys are ignored

Keys that aren't part of the schema are silently dropped when a file is loaded, so a misspelled or misplaced key (for example a z_plan placed directly on a stage position, rather than inside its sequence) won't raise an error. It's worth checking the loaded sequence (list(seq), or seq.sizes) before running it.

items.title: What about useq.v2?
items.text: useq.v2 is a preview of the next version of the API (with user-defined axes, among other things). useq.MDASequence, as described on these pages, is unchanged, and nothing needs to migrate yet. See useq-schema v2 (preview) if you're curious.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Building Sequences: common experiments, step by step.
  • The MDASequence, MDAEvent, axes and autofocus reference pages.
  • The Acquisition Engine, to run a sequence on a microscope.

items.title: useq-schema v2 (Preview)
items.text:
This is a preview

useq.v2 is a preview of the next version of the useq-schema API, and it may still change. useq.MDASequence, as described in the rest of these docs, is unchanged, and nothing needs to migrate yet.

pymmcore-plus can already run a useq.v2.MDASequence, but (for now) it treats it like any other iterable of events. The engine doesn't see the sequence itself, and saved data is written as one flat stack of frames.

In useq.MDASequence, the axes are fixed: time, positions, grid, channels and z ("tpgcz"), and the logic for combining them lives inside useq. In useq.v2, a sequence is a tuple of axes, and any object that follows the v2.AxisIterable interface can be one (it has an axis_key, yields values, and says what each value contributes to an event). The familiar plans (time plans, z plans, grids, channels, stage positions) are all v2 axes, so the same experiments can still be described, but you can also add your own axes, decide per axis which combinations to skip, give a single position its own plans, and post-process the stream of events with transforms.

The examples below all run against the current preview.

items.title: The old arguments still work
items.text:
v2.MDASequence accepts the same keyword arguments as useq.MDASequence, and converts them into axes:

from useq import v2

seq = v2.MDASequence(
    time_plan={"interval": 1.0, "loops": 2},
    stage_positions=[(10, 20, 5)],
    channels=["DAPI", "FITC"],
    z_plan={"range": 2, "step": 1},
)
print([str(axis.axis_key) for axis in seq.axes])
# ['t', 'p', 'c', 'z']

# ... which is the same as:
seq2 = v2.MDASequence(
    axes=(
        v2.TIntervalLoops(interval=1.0, loops=2),
        v2.StagePositions(values=[v2.Position(x=10, y=20, z=5)]),
        v2.ChannelsPlan(values=[v2.Channel(config="DAPI"), v2.Channel(config="FITC")]),
        v2.ZRangeAround(range=2, step=1),
    ),
)
assert list(seq) == list(seq2)

An existing useq.MDASequence can be converted with v2.MDASequence.model_validate(old_sequence). The events are the same as the ones useq.MDASequence yields (except that v2 events don't carry a reference to their sequence), with these exceptions in the current preview:

  • The Channel options acquire_every, do_stack and z_offset are not applied yet, so every channel is acquired at every time point and z position.
  • Giving a position its own sub-sequence with Position(sequence=...) emits a DeprecationWarning; see below for the v2 way.

items.title: Custom axes
items.text:
An axis yields values, and its contribute_to_mda_event method says what each value adds to the event. For example, here's an axis that steps a laser power (as a device property):

from collections.abc import Mapping

from useq import v2


class LaserPowerAxis(v2.SimpleValueAxis[float]):
    axis_key: str = "laser"

    def contribute_to_mda_event(self, value: float, index: Mapping[str, int]) -> dict:
        return {"properties": [("Laser", "Power", value)]}  # (1)!


seq = v2.MDASequence(
    axes=(
        v2.ChannelsPlan(values=["DAPI", "FITC"]),
        LaserPowerAxis(values=[10, 50]),
    ),
)
for event in seq:
    print(event)
  1. Whatever this returns is passed to MDAEvent(...). (For type checkers, the return type is MDAEvent.Kwargs, a TypedDict that only exists when type checking.)
index={'c': 0, 'laser': 0} channel=Channel(config='DAPI') properties=[PropertyTuple(device_name='Laser', property_name='Power', property_value=10.0)]
index={'c': 0, 'laser': 1} channel=Channel(config='DAPI') properties=[PropertyTuple(device_name='Laser', property_name='Power', property_value=50.0)]
index={'c': 1, 'laser': 0} channel=Channel(config='FITC') properties=[PropertyTuple(device_name='Laser', property_name='Power', property_value=10.0)]
index={'c': 1, 'laser': 1} channel=Channel(config='FITC') properties=[PropertyTuple(device_name='Laser', property_name='Power', property_value=50.0)]

v2.SimpleValueAxis iterates over a list of values. For anything else, subclass v2.AxisIterable and implement __iter__ (see Sequences that never end).

items.title: Skipping combinations
items.text:
Any axis can veto a combination of values by overriding should_skip. It receives a dict that maps each axis key to an (index, value, axis) tuple. Here the second channel gets a single plane rather than a z-stack:

from useq import v2


class SparseZ(v2.ZRangeAround):
    """Only take the full z-stack in the first channel."""

    def should_skip(self, prefix: dict) -> bool:
        c_index = prefix["c"][0]
        z_index = prefix["z"][0]
        return c_index > 0 and z_index != 1


seq = v2.MDASequence(
    axes=(
        v2.ChannelsPlan(values=["DAPI", "FITC"]),
        SparseZ(range=2, step=1),  # (1)!
    ),
)
for event in seq:
    print(event.index, event.channel.config, event.z_pos)
  1. There's no stage position here, so (just as in v1) this relative z plan is centered on z = 0, not on the current focus.
{'c': 0, 'z': 0} DAPI -1.0
{'c': 0, 'z': 1} DAPI 0.0
{'c': 0, 'z': 2} DAPI 1.0
{'c': 1, 'z': 1} FITC 0.0

items.title: Different plans for one position
items.text:
A value yielded by an axis may itself be a sequence, whose value stands in for the plain value, and whose axes replace (or add to) the parent's axes for that branch. Here, the second position gets a bigger z-stack:

from useq import v2

cell_1 = v2.MDASequence(
    value=v2.Position(x=100, y=100, z=10),
    axes=(v2.ZRangeAround(range=4, step=2),),
)

seq = v2.MDASequence(
    axes=(
        v2.StagePositions(values=[v2.Position(x=0, y=0, z=10), cell_1]),
        v2.ChannelsPlan(values=["DAPI"]),
        v2.ZRangeAround(range=1, step=1),
    ),
)
for event in seq:
    print(event.index, event.x_pos, event.z_pos)

{'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 0} 0.0 9.5
{'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 1} 0.0 10.5
{'p': 1, 'c': 0, 'z': 0} 100.0 8.0
{'p': 1, 'c': 0, 'z': 1} 100.0 10.0
{'p': 1, 'c': 0, 'z': 2} 100.0 12.0

items.title: Transforms
items.text:
Transforms see each event after it has been built, and may change it, drop it, or add more events, which makes it possible to insert events that don't belong to any axis. A transform is a callable that returns (or yields) events. It also gets the previous event, and a function that builds the next one, for look-ahead:

from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable

from useq import v2


class SnapBrightfieldAfterStack:
    """After each z-stack, add a single brightfield image."""

    def __call__(
        self,
        event: v2.MDAEvent,
        *,
        prev_event: v2.MDAEvent | None,
        make_next_event: Callable[[], v2.MDAEvent | None],
    ) -> Iterable[v2.MDAEvent]:
        yield event
        next_event = make_next_event()
        if next_event is None or next_event.index.get("z", 0) == 0:
            yield event.model_copy(
                update={"channel": v2.EventChannel(config="BF"), "z_pos": None}
            )


seq = v2.MDASequence(
    channels=["DAPI"],
    stage_positions=[(0, 0, 10), (100, 100, 10)],
    z_plan={"range": 2, "step": 1},
    transforms=(SnapBrightfieldAfterStack(),),
)
for event in seq:
    print(event.index, event.channel.config, event.z_pos)

{'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 0} DAPI 9.0
{'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 1} DAPI 10.0
{'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 2} DAPI 11.0
{'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 2} BF None
{'p': 1, 'c': 0, 'z': 0} DAPI 9.0
{'p': 1, 'c': 0, 'z': 1} DAPI 10.0
{'p': 1, 'c': 0, 'z': 2} DAPI 11.0
{'p': 1, 'c': 0, 'z': 2} BF None

Some of v1's built-in behavior is implemented as transforms, which v2 adds for you: ResetEventTimerTransform (when there is a time plan), and KeepShutterOpenTransform and AutoFocusTransform (when you set keep_shutter_open_across or autofocus_plan).

Warning

Passing transforms= replaces the default transforms. If your sequence has a time plan, add v2.ResetEventTimerTransform() to your own tuple, or the first event will no longer reset the event timer.

items.title: Sequences that never end
items.text:
v2 axes don't need a length, so a sequence can go on forever (or until the acquisition is cancelled):

import itertools
from collections.abc import Iterator, Mapping

from useq import v2


class Forever(v2.AxisIterable[int]):
    """A time axis with no end."""

    axis_key: str = "t"

    def __iter__(self) -> Iterator[int]:
        yield from itertools.count()

    def contribute_to_mda_event(self, value: int, index: Mapping[str, int]) -> dict:
        return {"min_start_time": value * 5.0}


seq = v2.MDASequence(axes=(Forever(), v2.ChannelsPlan(values=["DAPI", "FITC"])))
print(seq.is_finite())  # False
for event in itertools.islice(seq, 5):
    print(event.index, event.channel.config, event.min_start_time)

{'t': 0, 'c': 0} DAPI 0.0
{'t': 0, 'c': 1} FITC 0.0
{'t': 1, 'c': 0} DAPI 5.0
{'t': 1, 'c': 1} FITC 5.0
{'t': 2, 'c': 0} DAPI 10.0

items.title: Other kinds of events
items.text:
v2.MDASequence builds MDAEvent objects, but the class it is built on, v2.MultiAxisSequence, can build anything. Pass it an event_builder, which is called with the axes index (and the chain of enclosing sequences) for each combination:

from useq import v2


class DictBuilder:
    def __call__(self, axes_index: dict, context: tuple) -> dict:
        return {key: value for key, (index, value, axis) in axes_index.items()}


seq = v2.MultiAxisSequence(
    axes=(
        v2.SimpleValueAxis(axis_key="a", values=[1, 2]),
        v2.SimpleValueAxis(axis_key="b", values=["x", "y"]),
    ),
    event_builder=DictBuilder(),
)
print(list(seq.iter_events()))
# [{'a': 1, 'b': 'x'}, {'a': 1, 'b': 'y'}, {'a': 2, 'b': 'x'}, {'a': 2, 'b': 'y'}]

  • event - the current (already built) event.
  • prev_event - the previously transformed event that was just yielded, or None if this is the first call.
  • make_next_event - a zero-argument callable that lazily builds the next raw event (i.e. before any transformers). Only call it if you really need look-ahead so the pipeline stays lazy.

The transformer must return a list.

Return one event in the list for a 1-to-1 mapping, an empty list to drop the original event, or a list with multiple items to insert extras.

Iterate over the axes and yield combinations with context.

Yields:

Type Description AxesIndexWithContext

A tuple of (AxesIndex, MultiAxisSequence) where AxesIndex is a dictionary mapping axis keys to tuples of (index, value, AxisIterable), and MultiAxisSequence is the context that generated this axes combination. For example, when iterating over an AxisIterable with a single axis "t", with values of [0.1, .2], the yielded tuples would be: - ({'t': (0, 0.1, )}, ) - ({'t': (1, 0.2, )}, )

The base implementation aggregates transforms from outer to inner sequences. Only a single instance of each transform type is kept, so if multiple sequences in the context have the same transform type, only one will be used, and innermost MultiAxisSequence's transform will take precedence.

items.title: RandomPoints
items.text:
Bases: MultiPositionPlan

Yield random points in a specified geometric shape.

Attributes:

Name Type Description num_points int

Number of points to generate.

max_width float

Maximum width of the bounding box in microns.

max_height float

Maximum height of the bounding box in microns.

shape Shape

Shape of the bounding box. Current options are "ellipse" and "rectangle".

random_seed int | None

Random numpy seed that should be used to generate the points. If None, a random seed will be used.

allow_overlap bool

By default, True. If False and fov_width and fov_height are specified, points will not overlap and will be at least fov_width and fov_height apart.

order TraversalOrder | None

Order in which the points will be visited. If None, order is simply the order in which the points are generated (random). Use 'nearest_neighbor' or 'two_opt' to order the points in a more structured way.

start_at Position | int

Position or index of the point to start at. This is only used if order is 'nearest_neighbor' or 'two_opt'. If a position is provided, it will always be included in the list of points. If an index is provided, it must be less than the number of points, and corresponds to the index of the (randomly generated) points; this likely only makes sense when random_seed is provided.

axis_key Literal[<Axis.GRID: 'g'>]

A string id representing the axis.

fov_width float | None fov_height float | None

items.title: Building Sequences
items.text:
For most standard multi-dimensional experiments, you will want to use useq.MDASequence to construct your sequence of events. It allows you to declare a "plan" for each axis in your experiment (channels, time, z, etc...) along with the order in which the axes should be iterated. Iterating over the sequence yields useq.MDAEvent objects (usually one per image), so list(sequence) shows you which events an acquisition engine will be asked to run.

A sequence is just data, so you can build and inspect the examples on this page without a microscope. To run a sequence, see The Acquisition Engine.

items.title: Axes and plans
items.text:
Each axis has a field on MDASequence, and a one-letter key that is used in axis_order and in the index of each event:

key field describes reference t time_plan time points (interval, duration, number of loops, or several phases) time plans p stage_positions a list of stage positions (or a well plate) Position, well plates g grid_plan a grid (or random points) at each position grid plans c channels a list of channel presets, each with an optional exposure Channel z z_plan a z-stack z plans

axis_order (default "tpgcz") says how the axes are nested (the "fastest" axes come last). There are also a few fields that aren't axes, such as autofocus_plan (hardware autofocus), keep_shutter_open_across, setup, and metadata. See the MDASequence reference for all of them.

Let's look at how MDASequence can be used to create a few common experiments.

items.title: A two-channel time series
items.text:
from useq import MDASequence

mda_sequence = MDASequence(
    time_plan={"interval": 2, "loops": 6},  # (1)!
    channels=[
        {"config": "DAPI", "exposure": 50},
        {"config": "FITC", "exposure": 80},
    ],
)
  1. 6 time points, 2 seconds apart. See also, additional time plans.
output of list(mda_sequence)

Relative to what?

Most z plans (range, above/below, relative positions) and grid plans (rows/columns, width/height, random points) are relative: they are added to the z (or x/y) of each stage position. If a position doesn't specify z, or there are no stage_positions at all, a relative z plan is centered on z = 0, not on the current focus position:

>>> [e.z_pos for e in MDASequence(z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 1})]
[-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0]

(A relative grid with no x/y is likewise centered on x = y = 0.) On a real microscope, that may send the objective somewhere you didn't expect. So when you want a z-stack "around where I am now", put the current position in the sequence, e.g. with pymmcore-plus:

MDASequence(
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 1},
    stage_positions=[Position(z=core.getZPosition())],
)

(Absolute plans, like ZTopBottom or ZAbsolutePositions, aren't affected.)

items.title: A grid of z-stacks
items.text:
Here we use axis_order to declare that we want the full z-stack to happen at each (row, col) before moving to the next position in the grid.

from useq import MDASequence

mda_sequence = MDASequence(
    stage_positions=[{"x": 100, "y": 200, "z": 300}],
    grid_plan={"fov_width": 20, "fov_height": 10, "rows": 2, "columns": 2},
    z_plan={"range": 10, "step": 2.5},
    axis_order="pgz",  # (1)!
)
  1. The "fastest" axes come last. By putting z after g in the axis_order, we're saying "at each g, do a full z iteration".

items.title: Skipping timepoints or z-stacks
items.text:
The Channel field has a few tricks, such as skipping timepoints or z-stacks for specific channels. Here we take a fast z-stack (leaving the shutter open) in the FITC channel only, and a single image in the DIC channel every 3 timepoints:

from useq import MDASequence

mda_sequence = MDASequence(
    z_plan={"range": 10, "step": 2.5},  # (1)!
    time_plan={"interval": 2, "loops": 6},
    channels=[
        "FITC",
        {"config": "DIC", "acquire_every": 3, "do_stack": False},
    ],
    keep_shutter_open_across=["z"],
)
  1. There are no stage positions here, so the stack is centered on z = 0 (see above).
output of list(mda_sequence) (first two timepoints) 
[
    MDAEvent(
        index={"t": 0, "c": 0, "z": 0},

        reset_event_timer=True,
    ),

items.title: Different plans at different positions
items.text:
A stage position may carry its own sequence, whose plans replace the global ones at that position (any plan it doesn't set comes from the main sequence). Here, the second position gets a different z-stack:

from useq import MDASequence

mda_sequence = MDASequence(
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 1},
    stage_positions=[
        {"x": 0, "y": 0, "z": 10},
        {
            "name": "Cell 1",
            "x": 100,
            "y": 50,
            "z": 12,
            "sequence": {"z_plan": {"above": 2, "below": 0, "step": 0.5}},
        },
    ],
)

for event in mda_sequence:
    print(event.index, event.pos_name, event.z_pos)
output 
{'p': 0, 'z': 0} None 8.0
{'p': 0, 'z': 1} None 9.0
{'p': 0, 'z': 2} None 10.0
{'p': 0, 'z': 3} None 11.0
{'p': 0, 'z': 4} None 12.0
{'p': 1, 'z': 0} Cell 1 12.0
{'p': 1, 'z': 1} Cell 1 12.5
{'p': 1, 'z': 2} Cell 1 13.0
{'p': 1, 'z': 3} Cell 1 13.5
{'p': 1, 'z': 4} Cell 1 14.0

Note

pymmcore-plus can't yet save a sequence like this one as a multi-dimensional array (the positions don't share one shape), so it writes the frames as a flat stack. A sub-sequence that only adds a grid_plan is fine.

items.title: A note on syntax
items.text:
If you prefer, you can use useq objects rather than dicts for all of these fields. This has the advantage of providing type-checking and auto-completion in your IDE.

Example

The following two sequences are equivalent:

import useq

mda_sequence1 = useq.MDASequence(
    time_plan={"interval": 2, "loops": 10},
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 0.5},
    channels=[
        {"config": "DAPI", "exposure": 50},
        {"config": "FITC", "exposure": 80},
    ],
)

mda_sequence2 = useq.MDASequence(
    time_plan=useq.TIntervalLoops(interval=2, loops=10),
    z_plan=useq.ZRangeAround(range=4, step=0.5),
    channels=[
        useq.Channel(config="DAPI", exposure=50),
        useq.Channel(config="FITC", exposure=80),
    ],
)

assert mda_sequence1 == mda_sequence2

items.title: Saving and loading sequences
items.text:
MDASequence objects can be serialized and deserialized to and from JSON or YAML, making it easy to save and load them from file:

from pathlib import Path

import useq

mda_sequence = useq.MDASequence(
    stage_positions=[(100, 100, 30)],
    time_plan={"interval": 2, "loops": 10},
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 0.5},
    channels=[
        {"config": "DAPI", "exposure": 50, "do_stack": False},
        {"config": "FITC", "exposure": 20},
    ],
    axis_order="tpcz",
)

Path("mda_sequence.yaml").write_text(mda_sequence.yaml())

... results in:

mda_sequence.yaml
axis_order:
- t
- p
- c
- z
channels:
- config: DAPI
  do_stack: false
  exposure: 50.0
- config: FITC
  exposure: 20.0
stage_positions:
- x: 100.0
  y: 100.0
  z: 30.0
time_plan:
  interval: 2.0
  loops: 10
z_plan:
  range: 4.0
  step: 0.5

... which can be loaded back into an MDASequence object:

mda_sequence = useq.MDASequence.from_file("mda_sequence.yaml")

For JSON, use mda_sequence.model_dump_json(exclude_unset=True) to write and the same from_file (with a .json extension) to read. Only the fields you set are written, so the files stay short and readable. The overview has a larger example file, with multi-phase time plans and per-position z-stacks.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
Once you have a sequence, you'll probably want to run it:

  • The Acquisition Engine runs an MDASequence (or any iterable of MDAEvent) on a Micro-Manager-controlled microscope, and Saving Data shows how to write the images to OME-Zarr or OME-TIFF.
  • The MDASequence, MDAEvent and axes reference pages describe every field.

items.text: The following objects may be used to describe iteration over specific types of dimensions: the stage positions, channels, time plans, z plans, grids and well plates of an MDASequence. (Most of them may also be given as plain dicts, see Building Sequences.)

items.title: useq.ZTopBottom
items.text:
Bases: ZPlan

Define Z using absolute top & bottom positions.

Note that bottom will always be visited, regardless of go_up, while top will always be encompassed by the range, but may not be precisely visited if the step size does not divide evenly into the range.

Attributes:

Name Type Description top float

Top position in microns (inclusive).

bottom float

Bottom position in microns (inclusive).

step float

Step size in microns.

go_up bool

If True, instructs engine to start at bottom and move towards top. By default, True.

items.title: useq.ZAboveBelow
items.text:
Bases: ZPlan

Define Z as asymmetric range above and below some reference position.

Note that below will always be visited, regardless of go_up, while above will always be encompassed by the range, but may not be precisely visited if the step size does not divide evenly into the range.

Attributes:

Name Type Description above float

Range above reference position in microns (inclusive).

below float

Range below reference position in microns (inclusive).

step float

Step size in microns.

go_up bool

If True, instructs engine to start at bottom and move towards top. By default, True.

items.text:

Attributes:

Name Type Description absolute list[float]

List of absolute z positions.

go_up bool

If True (the default), visits points in the order provided, otherwise in reverse.

items.title: useq.ZRangeAround
items.text:
Bases: ZPlan

Define Z as a symmetric range around some reference position.

Note that -range / 2 will always be visited, regardless of go_up, while +range / 2 will always be encompassed by the range, but may not be precisely visited if the step size does not divide evenly into the range.

Attributes:

Name Type Description range float

Range in microns (inclusive). For example, a range of 4 with a step size of 1 would visit [-2, -1, 0, 1, 2].

step float

Step size in microns.

go_up bool

If True, instructs engine to start at bottom and move towards top. By default, True.

items.title: useq.ZRelativePositions
items.text:
Bases: ZPlan

Define Z as a list of positions relative to some reference.

Typically, the "reference" will be whatever the current Z position is at the start of the sequence.

Attributes:

Name Type Description relative list[float]

List of relative z positions.

go_up bool

If True (the default), visits points in the order provided, otherwise in reverse.

The bounded area is defined by top, left, bottom and right edges in stage coordinates. The bounds define the outer edges of the images, including the field of view and overlap.

Left stage position of the bounding area

Right stage position of the bounding area

items.title: useq.RandomPoints
items.text:
Yield random points in a specified geometric shape.

Attributes:

Name Type Description num_points int

Number of points to generate.

max_width float

Maximum width of the bounding box in microns.

max_height float

Maximum height of the bounding box in microns.

shape Shape

Shape of the bounding box. Current options are "ellipse" and "rectangle".

random_seed int | None

Random numpy seed that should be used to generate the points. If None, a random seed will be used.

allow_overlap bool

By default, True. If False and fov_width and fov_height are specified, points will not overlap and will be at least fov_width and fov_height apart.

order TraversalOrder | None

Order in which the points will be visited. If None, order is simply the order in which the points are generated (random). Use 'nearest_neighbor' or 'two_opt' to order the points in a more structured way.

start_at RelativePosition | int

Position or index of the point to start at. This is only used if order is 'nearest_neighbor' or 'two_opt'. If a position is provided, it will always be included in the list of points. If an index is provided, it must be less than the number of points, and corresponds to the index of the (randomly generated) points; this likely only makes sense when random_seed is provided.

fov_width float | None fov_height float | None

items.title: useq.GridFromPolygon
items.text:
Grid plan based on a polygon boundary.

This grid plan generates absolute stage positions that cover a polygon region. Additionally the convex hull, and/or a buffered polygon can be created to generate tiles over a larger area surrounding the initial polygon.

Attributes:

Name Type Description vertices list[tuple[float, float]]

List of (x, y) points that define the polygon boundary. Must have at least 3 points.

convex_hull bool | None

If True, the convex hull of the polygon will be used.

Expand area bounded by vertices to include all points within a offset of the original boundary. A positive offset produces a dilation, a negative offset an erosion.

overlap tuple[float, float]

mode OrderMode

Define the ways of ordering the grid positions. Options are row_wise, column_wise, row_wise_snake, column_wise_snake and spiral. By default, row_wise_snake.

fov_width float | None

Width of the field of view in microns. If not provided, acquisition engines should use current width of the FOV based on the current objective and camera. Engines MAY override this even if provided.

fov_height float | None

Height of the field of view in microns. If not provided, acquisition engines should use current height of the FOV based on the current objective and camera. Engines MAY override this even if provided.

items.title: useq.WellPlatePlan
items.text:
Bases: UseqModel, Sequence[Position]

A plan for acquiring images from a multi-well plate.

Attributes:

Name Type Description plate WellPlate

The well-plate definition. Minimally including rows, columns, and well spacing. If expressed as a string, it is assumed to be a key in useq.registered_well_plate_keys.

a1_center_xy tuple[float, float]

The stage coordinates in µm of the center of well A1 (top-left corner).

rotation float | None

The rotation angle in degrees (anti-clockwise) of the plate. If None, no rotation is applied. If expressed as a string, it is assumed to be an angle with units (e.g., "5°", "4 rad", "4.5deg"). If expressed as an arraylike, it is assumed to be a 2x2 rotation matrix [[cos, -sin], [sin, cos]], or a 4-tuple (cos, -sin, sin, cos).

selected_wells tuple[tuple[int, ...], tuple[int, ...]] | None

Any <=2-dimensional index expression for selecting wells. for example: - None -> No wells are selected. - slice(0) -> (also) select no wells. - slice(None) -> Selects all wells. - 0 -> Selects the first row. - [0, 1, 2] -> Selects the first three rows. - slice(1, 5) -> selects wells from row 1 to row 4. - (2, slice(1, 4)) -> select wells in the second row and only columns 1 to 3. - ([1, 2], [3, 4]) -> select wells in (row, column): (1, 3) and (2, 4)

well_points_plan GridRowsColumns | GridWidthHeight | RandomPoints | RelativePosition

A plan for acquiring images within each well. This can be a single position (for a single image per well), a GridRowsColumns (for a grid of images), or RandomPoints (for random points within each well).

The number of rows in the plate. Must be > 0.

The number of columns in the plate. Must be > 0.

The center-to-center distance in mm (pitch) between wells in the x and y directions. If a single value is provided, it is used for both x and y.

well_size tuple[float, float]

The size in mm of each well in the x and y directions. If the well is squared or rectangular, this is the width and height of the well. If the well is circular, this is the diameter. If a single value is provided, it is used for both x and y.

circular_wells bool

Whether wells are circular (True) or squared/rectangular (False).

A name for the plate.

Register well-plate definitions to allow lookup by key.

Added keys will override existing keys if they already exist.

Values may either be WellPlate instances, or dictionaries with the following keys: - rows: Required[int] - columns: Required[int] - well_spacing: Required[tuple[float, float]] - well_size: tuple[float, float] | None - circular_wells: bool - name: str

>>> useq.register_well_plates(

...         "custom-square-plate": {

...         },

...     }
... )

items.title: Event
items.text: An MDAEvent describes one thing for the microscope to do (usually: acquire an image), and the hardware state to do it in. Fields that are left as None mean "use the current setting". Iterating over an MDASequence yields events, but you can also create them yourself.

items.title: useq.MDAEvent
items.text:
Bases: UseqModel

Define a single event in a MDASequence.

Usually, this object will be generated by iterating over a MDASequence (see useq.MDASequence.iter_events).

Attributes:

Name Type Description index ReadOnlyDict

Index of this event in the sequence. This is a mapping of axis name to index. For example: {'t': 4, 'c': 0, 'z': 5}.

channel Channel | None

Channel to use for this event. If None, implies use current channel. By default, None. Channel is a simple pydantic object with two attributes: config and group. config is the name of the configuration to use for this channel, (e.g. "488nm", "DAPI", "FITC"). group is the name of the group to which this channel belongs. By default, "Channel".

exposure float | None

Exposure time in milliseconds. If not provided, implies use current exposure time. By default, None.

min_start_time float | None

Minimum start time of this event, in seconds. If provided, the engine will pause until this time has elapsed before starting this event. Times are relative to the start of the sequence, or the last event with reset_event_timer set to True.

pos_name str | None

The name assigned to the position. By default, None.

x_pos float | None

X position in microns. If not provided, implies use current position. By default, None.

y_pos float | None

Y position in microns. If not provided, implies use current position. By default, None.

z_pos float | None

Z position in microns. If not provided, implies use current position. By default, None.

slm_image SLMImage | None

Image data to display on an SLM device. SLMImage is a simple pydantic object with two attributes: data and device. data is the image data (anything that can be cast to a numpy array), device is the name of the SLM device to use. If not provided, the "default" SLM device should be used. By default, None.

sequence MDASequence | None

A reference to the useq.MDASequence this event belongs to. This is a read-only attribute. By default, None.

properties list[PropertyTuple] | None

List of useq.PropertyTuple to set before starting this event. Where each item in the list is a 3-member named tuple of (device_name, property_name, property_value). This is inspired by micro-manager's Device Adapter API, but could be used to set arbitrary properties in any backend that supports the concept of devices that have properties with values. By default, None.

roi CameraROI | None

Camera region of interest. Accepts a CameraROI object or a bare tuple of (offset_x, offset_y, width, height) which will be automatically converted. By default, None.

metadata dict[str, Any]

Optional metadata to be associated with this event. This is the place for any user-defined data (for example, parameters that a custom acquisition engine needs).

action HardwareAutofocus | AcquireImage | CustomAction

The action to perform for this event. By default, useq.AcquireImage. Example of another action is useq.HardwareAutofocus which could be used to perform a hardware autofocus. For backwards compatibility, an action of None implies AcquireImage. You may use CustomAction to indicate any custom action, with the data attribute containing any data required to perform the custom action.

keep_shutter_open bool

If True, the illumination shutter should be left open after the event has been executed, otherwise it should be closed. By default, False. This is useful when the sequence of events being executed use the same illumination scheme (such as a z-stack in a single channel), and closing and opening the shutter between events would be slow.

reset_event_timer bool

If True, the engine should reset the event timer to the time of this event, and future min_start_time values will be relative to this event. By default, False.

Bases: FrozenModel

Base class for a useq.MDAEvent action.

An Action specifies what task should be performed during a useq.MDAEvent. An Action can be for example used to acquire an image (useq.AcquireImage) or to perform a hardware autofocus (useq.HardwareAutofocus). An action of None implies AcquireImage.

You may use CustomAction to indicate any custom action, with the data attribute containing any data required to perform the custom action.

useq.Action to perform a hardware autofocus.

See also useq.AutoFocusPlan.

Attributes:

Name Type Description type Literal['hardware_autofocus']

This action can be used to trigger hardware autofocus.

autofocus_device_name str | None

The name of the autofocus offset motor device (if applicable). If None, acquisition engines may attempt to set the offset however they see fit (such as using a current or default autofocus device.)

Before autofocus is performed, the autofocus motor should be moved to this offset, if applicable. (Not all autofocus devices have an offset motor.) If None, the autofocus motor should not be moved.

This is a generic user action that can be used to represent anything that is not covered by the other action types, such as a microfluidic event, or a photostimulation, etc...

The data attribute is a dictionary that can contain any data that is needed to perform the custom action. It must be serializable to JSON by pydantic.

This action can be used to perform a custom action.

Custom data associated with the action.
